With as long as Detroit’s injury report has been recently, it got a little longer with Cade Cunningham as a late addition tonight. After the Pistons’ big win against San Antonio last night, it’s no surprise Deuce got some rest on the second night of a back-to-back.

JB Bickerstaff, with his shorthanded roster, rolled out the unusual starting lineup of Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Huerter, Javonte Green, Ausar Thompson, and John Collins. This would’ve been a great game for Ebuka Okorie to get some minutes, but he hurt his hip with the Motor City Cruise just the other day.

This meant Detroit’s key bench pieces were Paul Reed, Chaz Lanier, and Elijah Harkless. Even Tolu Smith saw some spot minutes when Collins and Reed both needed rest. Luckily, Isaiah Joe made his return to the lineup tonight after missing the last several games. Despite having to play guys from the end of the bench and on two-way spots, Detroit didn’t struggle against New Orleans.

Remember that unusual starting lineup for Detroit? Well, every single one of them finished in double digits. Jenkins, Green, and Collins all made at least three three-pointers. Jenkins, Thompson, and Huerter all had at least four assists, though Huerter had seven and DJ added nine.

Both Lanier and Joe made three three-pointers off the bench. Reed was the key sixth man once again, though that’s not all that peculiar nowadays. Harkless played his most minutes so far this season and did a great job sharing the rock with four assists.

In a game without their star player, this was another complete team win. There’s no doubt the depth on this team is one of the best in the league, and Detroit had seven different players score in double digits. Your Detroit Pistons are now 10-4 on the year.

Be sure you didn’t miss the lob finish by Woo:

For their next game, Detroit will host the Toronto Raptors on Friday, November 20th on Amazon Prime Video.

Shoutout to Joe Dumars and Troy Weaver – sounds like everything is going just swell down there in New Orleans.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs. Pelicans preview:  Closing out the road trip in New Orleans
pistons.body:
The Pistons have played a lot of road games so far this season.  They have also played less games than a lot of other teams because of that.  Last night’s game against the San Antonio Spurs was probably their toughest test of the season so far, and they passed it with flying colors.

The Spurs were in the midst of a 12 game winning streak and playing at home against a Pistons team down 4 players who were in their opening night rotation.  Despite that, they went into San Antonio and imposed their will and came out on top.

Now, they head to New Orleans to close out this 4-game road trip against a Pelicans team that has struggled this season.  After a game like last night, these are the exact kind of games that can be a bit of a trap, so hopefully the Pistons come out ready to play and close out this road trip with a 3-1 record.

The Pistons are still set to be short-handed, but as they proved last night, that doesn’t matter to this team.

Game Vitals

Where:  Smoothie King Center in New Orleans, LA
When:  Wednesday, November 18 at 8 pm EST
Watch:  Scripps Sports Network
Odds:  Pistons (-7.5)

Analysis

I mentioned the Pistons injuries above, as they are expected to once again be without Isaiah Joe, Duncan Robinson, Taurean Prince, Ron Holland, and Jalen Duren.  However, New Orleans is also without a slew of rotation players like Benedict Mathurin, Trey Murphy III, and Dejounte Murray.  The biggest difference is the Pistons have one of the deepest rosters in the league to overcome missing some key players while the Pelicans have a less talented roster.

None of that is to say that this game will be easy, but after a hard-fought battle against the Spurs last night, it will be nice to not have to deal with an imposing force like Victor Wembanyama again.

The Pistons depth was put to the test against the Spurs and the Pistons proved why they are one of the best teams in the Eastern Conference by coming out on top.  Of course, it was led by great 2-way performances by Cade Cunningham and Ausar Thompson, but that is to be expected of the Pistons two stars.

The Pelicans don’t present that same size-related issues the Pistons have had to deal with in their last few games, which is lucky for them.  The Pelicans do have a couple of players capable of taking over a game, like Jordan Poole and Zion Williamson, so it is important that the Pistons stay disciplined on defense, but Zion Williamson at least doesn’t tower over players like Ausar Thompson, who has had to take on more big matchups with the Pistons opting to start John Collins at center.

The Collins at center lineup has had a bit of diminishing returns lately as he has struggled to deal with size and rebounding, but it has allowed the Pistons to start Daniss Jenkins, who has been on a heater lately.  He had 25 points, 5 rebounds, and 5 assists last night against the Spurs and a couple of clutch shots.  He also had 21 and 22 points in back-to-back games against the Wizards after a 31 point game against the Lakers.  The Pistons will have a tough decision to make when Jalen Duren returns as they probably should continue to start Jenkins, but Duren doesn’t bring the same level of spacing as John Collins does and John Collins was signed to complement Jalen Duren at the four.

But, those are the good problems to have when you have a team as deep as the Pistons.

Another player to watch for the Pelicans is Jeremiah Fears, who had a triple-double in the Pelicans’ dismantling of the Golden State Warriors on Monday.  He is starting to put things together and develop into their future at point guard right at a time when Dejounte Murray has requested a trade.  Say what you want about the process in how the Pelicans have drafted and acquired picks in the last couple seasons, but they at least appear to have hit on Fears.

Another reclamation project they have hit on is former Piston, Saddiq Bey.  He earned an extension in the offseason after putting together a pretty solid season last year after recovering from the torn ACL he suffered a couple years ago.  As Pistons fans know, Bey is capable of getting hot, so he is another player they will have to look out for.

Overall, this shouldn’t be too difficult of a matchup for the Pistons, but after the emotions of a hard-fought battle last night, I would not be shocked to see a slow start out of the Pistons.  But, even with the injured players, the Pistons are the more talented team and should be able to win this game.

Lineups

Detroit Pistons (9-4):  Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Kevin Heurter, Ausar Thompson, John Collins

New Orleans Pelicans (5-10):  Jeremiah Fears, Herb Jones, Saddiq Bey, Zion Williamson, Yves Missi

pistons.body:
SAN ANTONIO, TX - NOVEMBER 17: Cade Cunningham #2 of the Detroit Pistons drives to the basket during the game against the San Antonio Spurs on November 17, 2026 at the Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, user is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. Mandatory Copyright Notice: Copyright 2026 NBAE (Photos by Michael Gonzales/NBAE via Getty Images) | NBAE via Getty Images

The Detroit Pistons played their best defensive game of the year to overwhelm the San Antonio Spurs en route to a 105-93 win in San Antonio. For the Pistons, it was a true return to the identity that has defined them during the JB Bickerstaff era. Play suffocating defense, never quit on any play, and attack the paint.

Some of those qualities have been absent this year with the loss of Jalen Duren down low. Combine that with going against the hottest team in the NBA with the most dominant big man since Shaquille O’Neal, and it seemed like a recipe for trouble.

Of course, what we should have all learned by now is that the moment you count out the Detroit Pistons is the moment they deliver their best performances.

The Pistons were led by a dominant back court of Cade Cunningham, the NBA superstar, and Daniss Jenkins, the most dangerous man in the first year of a real NBA contract after cutting his teeth in the G League. Cunningham scored 27 points and added six assists. Jenkins added 25 points and five assists.

They needed to deliver big time because the Pistons’ roster was depleted even more than normal. Detroit was not only without Duren down low, but they were also without their two most dangerous 3-point threats in Duncan Robinson and Isaiah Joe, and without one of the best defenders off the bench in the NBA, Ron Holland.

That didn’t matter, because every player on the Pistons roster understood how big this game was, and that if you want to call yourself an NBA title contender, you have to bring it against a powerhouse like the Spurs.

San Antonio entered tonight averaging 118.8 points per game, and before tonight, its lowest output of the season was 104 points against the Oklahoma City Thunder. To hold this Spurs team to more than 10 points below their previous low is a statement to the rest of the NBA. The Detroit Pistons can beat anyone on any night.

And anyone can be the hero. Paul Reed hit some huge acrobatic shots down low. Ausar Thompson almost had his second triple-double of November with 14 points, 12 assists, and nine rebounds. Thompson was matched up with Wembenyama on the night so that Wemby could play a roaming free safety. Detroit counteracted that by putting the ball in Ausar’s hands and using him a lot in pick-and-roll situations. Thompson was attacking early and finding open teammates throughout the night.

The Pistons outscored the Spurs in the paint 60-44 and in fast-break points 24-15. San Antonio is the lowest-turnover team in the NBA, but the Pistons were able to ratchet up the pressure, fight through screens, deflect handoffs and entry passes, and generate 10 steals. It was a total team effort from one of the best teams in the NBA.

pistons.headline: Pistons vs Spurs preview: No Duncan or Duren, others must step up
pistons.body:
The Detroit Pistons are down four rotation players as they match up with Tobias Harris and the San Antonio Spurs. Harris has not made his season debut due to a nagging calf injury. That hasn’t affected the Spurs in the slightest.

The absences of Duncan Robinson, Ron Holland, Isaiah Joe, and Jalen Duren surely make a difference for Detroit. The shooters will be extremely missed, with Victor Wembanyama’s presence shrinking the floor.

Duren has some eye-popping moments against the MVP candidate, but we won’t see that big man clash until late March, unless they line it up in the NBA cup Finals.

Jalen Duren dunks all over Wemby 😳 pic.twitter.com/zVaRSeZ4Ca
— Sportsnet (@Sportsnet) February 24, 2026

GAME VITALS

Where: Frost Bank Center, San Antonio, TX

When: 8 PM EST

Watch: Peacock NBC

Odds: Pistons (+9.5)

There aren’t too many games where Cade Cunningham doesn’t step on the floor as the guy. He can be him in any matchup, but it will take a lot to top Wemby. Considering how small Detroit is currently, their hands are full with the 7-foot-4 Frenchman.

John Collins started at the 5 over the last three games. With Robinson out, don’t be surprised if Paul Reed re-enters the starting group. That isn’t a Goliath pairing, but some teams opt for as much size as possible when defending Wemby.

The “put the small on Wemby” philosophy hasn’t been fruitful this year. Wemby is dunking everything. Per Basketball-Reference, 27 percent of his shots are slams. That’s way up from 18 percent last year. Detroit could have success “forcing” him to shoot. He’s shooting 32 percent on triples and 39 percent on all middies.

That’s a tough ask. Detroit’s defense came up short against Giannis Antetokounmpo and the Heat Saturday night. Giannis scored 24 points in the paint. That same type of shots-at-the-rim challenge is up tonight.

Here’s a glass-half-full takeaway from Collins. He’s made at least two 3s in each of the past three games. Yes, glass half full for sure. Plus, he is shooting 38 percent from 3 on the season. Teams haven’t cared, though. They still treat him like a maybe shooter. San Antonio will absolutely dare him to shoot from the wings tonight.

Detroit needs the open ones. Collins has to start hitting enough for teams to feel they need to stay attached. The defensive rotations can get better. The rim protection will not get better. That’s not who he is. He’s been disappointing defensively and on the glass. The shooting has to be feared enough to aid the spacing — high percentages on low volume won’t shift defenses.

The Spurs are the second-best defense in the league, only trailing the Minnesota Timberwolves. While Wemby suffocates you, the “smalls” relentlessly hound.

Stephon Castle and Dylan Harper are big guards who get after it. Castle especially is an All-Defense caliber guy. Cade plays to win, but he’ll want to let loose against Castle, who gave him trouble in the second February game last year.

Cade was better in the first one and led Detroit to the dub. He’ll try to do that again tonight with an undermanned roster.

Ausar Thompson will do some leading too, as he’s had the ball in his hands a lot more. According to Databallr, here’s his on-ball percentage by year:

2024: 9.3%

2025: 14.4%

2026: 17.6%

2027: 21.2%

Ausar got his first triple-double a few games ago. He was so involved, zipping up and down the floor. Detroit needs all of that and then some tonight. He has to stay on the floor.

In the dawg category, Daniss Jenkins is in the 100th percentile. He steps up whenever Detroit is counted out. No Robinson, so he’ll surely start. The Spurs don’t allow many 3s, so Jenkins needs to be ready to knock down when he gets his chances.

Jenkins creates a lot of chances with his I don’t care who’s guarding me mentality, so expect him to get them up, with the paint being limited.

You can’t fault his philosophy either. Jenkins is shooting 42 percent on five 3s a game. He makes them count. Detroit will need every ounce of his fearlessness as they travel to San Antonio. The Spurs are winners of 12 in a row. Detroit will rarely be nine-point underdogs. Let’s see how they come out in this position.

Projected starting lineup

Detroit Pistons (8-4): Cade Cunningham, Daniss Jenkins, Ausar Thompson, John Collins, Paul Reed

San Antonio Spurs (12-2): De’Aaron Fox, Dylan Harper, Stephon Castle, Devin Vassell, Victor Wembanyama

Question of the day

Who or what has been the most impressive in the No-Duren stretch?

pistons.headline: 3-man Fastbreak: Navigating without Duren
pistons.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 04: Jalen Duren #0 of the Detroit Pistons looks on from the bench during a game against the Philadelphia 76ers at Little Caesars Arena on November 04, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. NOTE TO USER: User expressly acknowledges and agrees that, by downloading and or using this photograph, User is consenting to the terms and conditions of the Getty Images License Agreement. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Sitting at 8-4, Detroit finds itself right under Boston and Philadelphia at the top of the conference – having already knocked off both squads. What makes that start even more impressive is how much of it has come with Jalen Duren sidelined by a hamstring issue.

It shouldn’t come as a shock to see the Pistons maintaining their place among the Eastern Conference elite, but the bigger story might be how long it takes the rest of the field to gel. Contenders like Indiana, Orlando, and Toronto entered the campaign with big ambitions, yet all three are currently stumbling below .500.

Here are a few key takeaways from this recent run of action.

1. Has the team’s limitations from last season changed?

Fresh off a impressive 60-win campaign, Detroit has quieted critics who viewed their summer moves with skepticism. Retaining their core talent with long-term deals has paid immediate dividends, as their roster continuity continues to fuel early momentum.

While the Pistons have routinely handled lesser opponents, their battles against heavyweights like New York, Philadelphia, and Los Angeles revealed familiar flaws. During offensive droughts, the ball movement stalled, resulting in over-reliance on Cade Cunningham to create individual magic while the surrounding unit remained static.

Is it a real cause for concern yet considering they’ve been down their second best player? Not in the short term.

This foundational identity guarantees postseason basketball and likely home-court advantage, yet doubts regarding their ceiling remain. Rumors of offseason trade pursuits suggest the front office recognizes the missing piece, but until a major acquisition materializes, lingering questions about their championship credentials will remain.

2. Inside -> out offense

Detroit’s identity remains largely unchanged from the past two seasons, but the offense is clearly evolving, especially without their All-NBA big man.

Last season, Detroit led the league with 57.9 points in the paint per game. This year, that figure has fallen to 47.2, around the middle of the pack. Duren’s absence since the second game has certainly played a role, but the shift also reflects the team’s offseason moves. Detroit moved on from Isaiah Stewart and Tobias Harris while adding better floor spacers in John Collins and Isaiah Jones. Duncan Robinson has also taken on a larger role, posting career highs with 17.4 points per game while shooting 43.1% from three.

That improved spacing has helped fuel Detroit’s early success, but defense remains the team’s foundation, with Detroit still leading the league in several defensive categories. Once Duren returns, it will be worth watching whether the offensive approach changes.

3. Dannis’s development

In the three games since Jenkins replaced Paul Reed in the starting lineup on November 8, Jenkins averaged 24.7 points, 5.7 rebounds, 4.0 assists, 2.3 steals and 4.3 three-pointers per game. The undrafted guard made occasional starts last season, but only when Cunningham was injured or resting. This year, the temporary promotion while Duren remains out shows that J.B. Bickerstaff trusts Jenkins with a larger role.

Since emerging in Detroit last season, Jenkins has gone from a promising two-way player to a legitimate contributor on a contending team. Jenkins has also shown a willingness to embrace any role and play with maximum effort. The question is no longer whether Jenkins can be a reliable role player, but how large that role can become as the stakes rise.

At 25, Jenkins still has room to grow. He is shooting 42.4% from three this season on 4.9 attempts per game and is averaging fewer turnovers than last year despite playing eight more minutes per night.

That chip on the shoulder may be Jenkins’ greatest strength, and continued growth could be an underrated factor in how far the Pistons go this season.

The Detroit Pistons face the Giannis-led Miami Heat for the second time this season, but this is not the same Heat team Detroit beat 128-111 in the second game of the season. The Heat can get above .500 with a win after winning six of its past eight games, including the previous three in a row. The Heat are starting to understand how best to play around Giannis Antetokounmpo, especially Bam Adebayo. In the team’s most recent win, Bam and Giannis scored 37 points, and Davion Mitchell was able to support the big two with a 22-point, 17-assist effort.

The Pistons also had Jalen Duren the last time the two teams faced each other, and the big man is still out, and Detroit’s big man is still out recovering from a hamstring injury. Detroit’s big men have been an issue since Duren went down, and that could be an issue when going against both Bam and Giannis. Of course, the Pistons do have Cade Cunningham, and he has vaulted himself into a top-10 player in the NBA. Cunningham is coming off a career-high 52 points and an NBA-first 50-point, 10-assist, zero-turnover game. lions.headline: NFL predictions: 4 keys to a Lions victory over the Buccaneers in Week 11
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 20: Amon-Ra St. Brown #14 of the Detroit Lions scores a touchdown in the first quarter against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field on October 20, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions (7-2) and Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) will face off at Ford Field in Detroit in a Week 11 showdown. The Lions and Bucs have faced each other four times in the last three seasons, and these two teams know each other almost as well as their head coaches.

“Tampa Bay Bucs, competitive, physical unit,” Lions coach Dan Campbell said of the Bucs. “Known (Buccaneers Head Coach) Todd Bowles a long time. Obviously have got a ton of respect for him and what he’s about. And this defense is playing outstanding football. And offensively, they’re committed to the run game, time of possession. They’re trying to force you into making errors. And really, the last three games, they played some pretty good football.”

This week’s prediction preview is sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, who currently have the Lions listed at +2000 to win this year’s Super Bowl and are currently 6.5-point favorites in Week 11. Let’s take a closer look at this matchup and predict how the Lions will beat the Bucs in this week’s Honolulu Blueprint.

Bucs base scheme

For a detailed look at the opposing scheme, check out our complementary breakdown piece: Lions Week 11 preview: Breaking down the Bucs’ offensive and defensive schemes.

Prediction 1: Lions continue to feed 14

Germany was a storybook celebration of Amon-Ra St. Brown. The Lions All-Pro receiver may have made only four receptions, but he chewed up 98 yards, and both touchdown receptions were epic.

As fantastic as Germany was for St. Brown, it’s not his only source of energy; he has a history of repeating big-game success against specific opponents. For example, St. Brown always shows up big when the Lions play the Bills, but after Buffalo, he’s consistently had the most success against the Buccaneers.

Over four games, St. Brown’s per-game averages include: 9.25 receptions, 101.5 receiving yards, and .75 touchdowns:

2025: 6 receptions, 86 yards, 1 touchdown

2024: 11 receptions, 119 yards

2023 (Playoffs): 8 receptions, 77 yards, 1 TD

2023: 12 receptions, 124 yards, 1 TD

The Bucs run a tight bump-and-run press at the line of scrimmage, and they operate out of zone coverage on nearly 85% of defensive snaps. St. Brown excels at beating press with his precision route running, quickness, and strength, and he’s often quarterback Jared Goff’s first read because the All-Pro receiver is elite at finding soft spots in the zone.

Add in the fact that the Bucs blitz nearly 44% of the time (second most in the NFL), and St. Brown will often set up behind the linebackers, secure catches in volume, and churn out yards after the catch (YAC). This is the fifth time in four years St. Brown has faced this defense, so he should have a strong feel for its weaknesses in zone.

Feed the hot hand.

Prediction 2: Gibbs attacks edges on the ground and through the air

Prediction No. 1 last week was to attack the edges of the Patriots’ defensive line, and it played out to perfection. This week, I am calling for it again, not only because it’s working, but it’s also worked in the past against this defense.

Here’s a look at Gibbs numbers from the last four games against the Bucs, noting that he was injured and inactive in the first meeting, and splitting touches with David Montgomery in the other three games:

2025: 17 rushes, 136 yards (8.0 ypc), 2 TDs — 3 receptions, 82 yards

2024: 13 rushes, 84 yards (6.5 ypc), 0 TDs — 7 receptions, 22 yards

2023 (P): 9 rushes, 74 yards (8.2 ypc), 1 TD — 4 receptions, 40 yards

2023: Inactive

Three things stand out when looking at those statistics: 1) the rushing yards per carry numbers are gaudy; 2) the Lions aren’t afraid to find Gibbs through the air, as it can be highly productive and effective in slowing down the Bucs’ blitz; and 3) if this is what he produced in a part-time role, can he exceed these numbers?

It would be a lofty expectation for Gibbs to maintain this level of success, especially since the Bucs allow only 79.1 rushing yards per game (best in the NFL), 3.5 yards per carry (3rd best), -0.13 EPA on runs against them (3rd), and a 38.3% rushing success rate (4th).

However, if we look back at the last five weeks (four games for the Bucs), Tampa Bay’s run defense numbers have been closer to average than elite: 87 rushing yards per game, 3.87 ypc (10th), -0.05 EPA on runs against (18th), and a 42.2% success rate (19th) allowed.

Over that same time period, the Lions have won five straight games, and Gibbs is averaging 99.2 yards per game (best in the NFL)—eclipsing 100 rushing yards in four of the last five games—, 5.28 yards per carry (5th), -0.02 EPA (9th), and a 43.6% success rate (10th).

The Bucs run defense is formidable, but they’ve been slightly vulnerable lately, and with the odds-on favorite for Offensive Player of the Year honors in your backfield (according to FanDuel Sportsbook), you need to get the ball into his hands.

Prediction 3: Lions load the box to stop the run

The Bucs rushing attack is one of the best in the NFL, and it’s carried the team through some rough patches. Statistically, they rank No. 1 in the NFL in rushing yards per game (163.9), rushing yards per play (5.0), explosive rushing plays over the last four games (16.1%), and 20+ yard runs (11). While some of those stats may be skewed by the “monsoon” game, where the Bucs attempted only three passes and ran the ball 56 times for 324 yards, they’re still in the top 5 in most rushing categories even without that anomaly.

The Bucs deploy a two-headed rushing attack with Bucky Irving and Kenneth Gainwell, but Irving is the starter and Tampa Bay will often ride his hot hand. Here’s Next Gen Stats with more on Irving:

“Bucky Irving enters Week 11 of 2026 with 825 rushing yards, 5th in the NFL, including two games with 150-plus rushing yards (tied for 2nd in the NFL, trailing only Jahmyr Gibbs with four). Irving has recorded seven scrimmage touchdowns since Week 5, tied for 2nd in the NFL behind only McCaffrey (9). His 91.7 rushing yards per game in 2026 would rank as the second-most in a single season in Buccaneers history, trailing only James Wilder’s 96.5 rush yards per game in 1984.”

The Bucs use a blend of blocking schemes, including outside zone, inside zone, and counter, but they lean most on “gap” concepts. According to Next Gen Stats, the Bucs utilize a gap blocking scheme on “29.7% of their designed carries (5th highest rate) and on these runs have recorded a league-leading 415 rushing yards,” with Irving accounting for over half that production (230 yards).

However, as Next Gen also points out, the Lions have done well against gap concepts this season, allowing only 3.3 yards per carry (6th fewest) and just one touchdown this season from this scheme. Overall, the Lions’ run defense has been steady and is improving as the season rolls on. They’re 5th in the NFL in yards allowed per game (90.4), No. 1 in preventing yards after contact, and in their last four games, they’ve allowed a rushing success rate of only 33.8% (3rd best).

This is a real strength-on-strength matchup, according to Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard:

“They’re the number one rush offense in the League and we’re one of the top premier run defenses in the League. […] They don’t hide it, and we don’t hide the way we play. So it’s a beautiful thing. It’s a beautiful challenge, and we’re looking forward to it.”

With the Bucs passing offense struggling (they’re bottom-five in most statistical categories) and the rushing attack being their biggest weapon, look for the Lions to load the box—potentially utilizing three safety sets following the return of Kerby Joseph—and lean on players like Brian Branch to live near the line of scrimmage and try to slow down Irving and the Bucs ‘ run game.

Prediction 4: Lions win turnover battle

The Bucs defense has been very opportunistic this season and currently leads the NFL with 21 forced turnovers (16 interceptions, 5 fumbles recovered) through nine games. They’re +7 overall in turnover ratio (3rd), as the Bucs offense has turned the ball over 14 times (9 interceptions, five fumbles lost).

The defense has been on fire of late. Of their 21 turnovers forced, 13 came in the last three games, including picking off Bears QB Caleb Williams four times in their last outing, and they’ve turned those turnovers into 57 points, the third-highest total in the NFL—that’s over 28% of their total points scored for the season (202).

“Well, they are opportunistic,” Campbell said of the Bucs ‘ ability to generate turnovers. “Obviously (Buccaneers Coach Todd Bowles) he’s always done it. He pressures a lot, throws a lot at you and forces you into errors, […] They’re well coached. The disguises are good. They’ve got a counter look for a look. They want to show you the picture, but now it could be three different coverages and pressures. So, they do a really good job of that, and that’s it. They want to force you into errors.”

Jared Goff’s first six games of the season were clean: no turnovers and 14 touchdowns. But Goff has run into some bad luck (Jameson Williams slipping on a route) and made a few questionable throws, resulting in four interceptions over the last three games. Overall, the Lions have done well in the turnover department this season and are +2 through nine games (13th). But they’ve also fumbled twice in the last month and are -2 net over the last four.

But the Lions offense isn’t alone with their recent struggles in this department: the Bucs offense has been loose with the ball. Baker Mayfield is dealing with a thumb injury in his throwing hand, is coming off a two-interception performance with wildly inconsistent accuracy, and had three fumbles the week prior in their “monsoon” game. Bucky Irving has also fumbled three times in the last three games (one in each), but has been fortunate to only lose one to the opponent.

The comfy confines of Ford Field and home-field advantage have favored the Lions, and in the four games they’ve played in Detroit, they’ve forced six turnovers (including at least one in each game) while giving up just four. Even a minor advantage or break-even scenario should be considered a win for the Lions because turnovers have played a big part in keeping the Bucs in games or letting them slip away, and the Lions won’t want to give them any chances to stick around in this one.

lions.headline: What game are you most looking forward to in Week 11?
lions.body:
With the calendar inching its way toward Thanksgiving, December football in the NFL is just around the corner. And with it, many division and playoff races begin to really heat up. As for the NFC North, things may be warmer than any other division in football. The Detroit Lions hold possession of first place as we head into Week 11, with the Minnesota Vikings and Chicago Bears right behind them, each with seven wins of their own. For Detroit, they will host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field this Sunday. Overall, Week 11 is a bit light in terms of games where both teams have playoff aspirations, but there are still plenty of games with intriguing storylines. Which Week 11 game are you most looking forward to?

lions.headline: Detroit Lions vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers preview, prediction: On Paper
lions.body:
Tampa Bay Buccaneers quarterback Baker Mayfield (6) hugs Detroit Lions quarterback Jared Goff (16) at the end of the Detroit Lions game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Ford Field in Detroit on Sunday, Sept. 15, 2024. Buccaneers won 20-16. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

For the first time in several weeks, the Detroit Lions hold the top spot in the NFC North. But in order to hold it, they’ll have to take down a sneaky-good Tampa Bay Buccaneers team. They may be 3-6 on the season, but as you’ll soon see, they are doing a lot of things very well, and present a tough matchup for any team. There’s a reason why they have a positive point differential, despite having two times the losses than wins.

I’ll break it down further in my Detroit Lions vs. Tampa Bay Buccaneers preview and prediction: On Paper.

Lions pass offense (11th) vs. Bucs pass defense (3rd)

The Lions’ passing attack remains pretty steady and reliable, despite the fact that Jared Goff has now thrown an interception in three straight games after not throwing a single one through his first six contests. For the year, the Lions rank:

Sixth in yards per attempt (8.0)

Fifth in passer rating (106.0)

Fifth in dropback EPA (0.200)

Fifth in success rate (49.9%)

In short, the Lions have been playing like a near top-five passing offense pretty much all season.

Goff is at his best when his offensive line is pass blocking for him, and the front has done a pretty good job this year. Detroit is allowing just a 30.8% pressure rate (fifth best) and 6.4% sack rate (15th), while ranking fourth in pass block win rate (58%) and second in PFF pass blocking grade (76.8).

Relevant this week is how Goff performs against the blitz, seeing as Tampa blitzes at the second-highest rate in the NFL. This year against the blitz, the Goff ranks:

Fifth in passer rating (115.6)

Fourth in EPA/dropback (+0.19)

Sixth in yards per pass attempt (8.2)

So blitz at your own peril.

The Bucs have shut down nearly every single opponent this year in the passing game, outside of—oddly—Deshaun Watson. For the year, they rank:

11th in yards per attempt (6.6)

Second in passer rating (72.7)

Second in dropback EPA (-0.101)

Eighth in success rate (43.3%)

Obviously, these stats are pretty darn good, but with lower success rates and yards per attempt than EPA and passer rating, there’s at least a little indication that some of these stats are being propped up by Tampa’s ridiculous 16 interceptions (most in NFL) and 5.2 interception rate (highest). While the Bucs deserve credit for those interceptions, a 5.2% interception rate is unbelievably high. The highest interception rate for an entire season over the past 10 years is 4.7%. There’s a good chance this is unsustainable.

Regardless, this is still a top-10 pass defense and shouldn’t be overlooked.

As mentioned earlier, the Bucs have the second-highest blitz rate (43.9%), yet their pressure rate ranks just 24th (33.2%) and their sack rate is 25th (5.0%) per NFL Pro. That said, they are improving as the season goes on. Of their 17 sacks on the season, 11 have come in the last four games.

Really, their pass defense is led by a strong secondary. Cornerbacks Jacob Parish, Zyon McCullom, and rookie nickel Keionte Scott are having outstanding seasons.

Player to watch: Rueben Bain Jr. vs. Blake Miller. Who isn’t excited about first-round rookie on rookie action? Bain and Miller were taken two spots apart, and both have had ups and downs in their rookie season. Bain is starting to put some things together after a slow start to his career, while Miller has seen more good than bad.

Advantage: Lions +0.5. With all due respect to DVOA, I think the Bucs’ numbers are a little artificially inflated by high interception rates. I still think it’s going to be a slog for the Lions to put up big numbers, but I won’t be surprised if they can patiently dink and dunk their way down the field.

Lions run offense (2nd) vs. Bucs run defense (5th)

Every week, the Lions’ run game gets a little more consistent and explosive. For the year, Detroit ranks:

Eighth in yards per carry (4.6)

10th in rush EPA (-0.021)

Second in success rate (47.1%)

What’s even more promising is that the high stuffed rate that had been plaguing this rushing attack is finally starting to settle down. Right now it sits at 18.6%, which is still 10th-highest, but it’s on a downward trajectory. Similarly, their power success rate is much better now. After Week 8, the Lions were converting on just 59% of short yardage situations (24th). Now they’re at 68% (12th).

It’s been a marriage between good blocking and Jahmyr Gibbs being outstanding. The Lions rank second in adjusted line yards (4.99), seventh in run block win rate (75%), and fourth in PFF run-blocking grade (77.0).

Meanwhile, Gibbs has forced 16 more missed tackles than any other player and is averaging 3.6 yards after contact per rush (11th).

Put it all together and Detroit is both extremely consistent down to down (see: success rate) and explosive (second-most 10+ yard runs in the NFL).

The Lions may have met their match this week. The Bucs haven’t allowed over 100 rushing yards since Week 1, and only two opponents all year have managed 4.0 yards per carry or more against this unit.

For the year, they rank:

Third in yards per carry allowed (3.5)

Third in rush EPA (-0.145)

Second in success rate (34.9%)

It’s hard to pick holes in the data here. Tampa is legit. They don’t give up big plays (only 16 rushes of 10+ yards, third fewest). The defensive line ranks well in run-stop win rate (eight), adjusted line yards (seventh), and second in PFF run-defense grade.

Player to watch: Josiah Trotter. The second-round rookie linebacker has been outstanding for the Bucs’ defense, ranking 19th in PFF run defense grade among qualifying linebackers. He leads the team in tackles (76) and PFF run stops (14).

Advantage: Draw. It’s elite vs. elite, and both teams have shown they can win those kind of matchups. Detroit ran all over the elite Vikings’ run defense, while the Bucs completely shut down both the Falcons and Bears strong rushing attacks. I can’t pick a side here.

Bucs pass offense (26th) vs. Lions pass defense (19th)

Bold and italicized data were starts by Jalen Daniels.

The Buccaneers’ passing attack has been a disaster this year, and it’s hard to figure out why. For the year, they rank:

29th in yards per attempt (5.9)

31st in passer rating (70.2)

30th in dropback EPA (-0.129)

31st in success rate (37.9%)

It’s been a disaster year for Baker Mayfield. Beyond just the injuries to his thumb and feet, Mayfield has just not looked the same as the game-changer he had been for the previous few years. Accuracy has been a problem, ranking 27th of 31 in completion percentage over expected (-3.3%). His PFF passing grade of 54.8 is 31st out of 37 qualifying QBs.

But his receiving corps hasn’t been much help, either. There just doesn’t seem to be any chemistry between quarterback and receiver.

Pass protection, however, has been acceptable. Tampa ranks 16th in pressure rate allowed (36.4%), 11th in pass-block win rate, and sixth in PFF pass-blocking grade (73.7). However, they have the second-highest sack rate (10.1%), suggesting both Mayfield and Daniels have struggled to escape pressure when it arrives.

For now, I’m assuming Mayfield plays in this game, but if Daniels has to go, it’s good news for Detroit. The rookie quarterback has an even worse CPOE (-5.7%) and worse passer rating (74.9 vs. 63.4).

I want to believe that the Lions’ pass defense is getting better, but it’s really hard to know. They’ve faced some very mediocre quarterbacks all season, and the numbers are certainly improving, but I can’t yet say it’s good. Even the data from the last two weeks comes with significant asterisks because of Malik Willis’ injury and Drake Maye exiting one series into the game.

Compiled on top of that are the injuries to Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson, but the returns of Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph are a factor, too, and there is just so much noise with the data here that it’s hard to make sense of anything.

For the year, Detroit ranks:

13th in yards per attempt allowed (7.0)

20th in passer rating (94.6)

24th in dropback EPA (0.125)

23rd in dropback success rate (47.6%)

Detroit has climbed out of the basement in a hurry, and if you were to just look at Detroit’s stats out of the bye week (Weeks 7-10), they’re even better:

Fourth in passer rating (75.2)

Seventh in dropback EPA (-0.045)

Fifth in dropback success rate (39.2%)

But, again, how much is this impacted by strength of opponent?

Pass rush will be a big question moving forward without Hutchinson. He was responsible for 52 of the teams’ 199 pressures—with Alim McNeill (39), Skyler Gill-Howard (19), DJ Wonnum (19), and Derrick Moore (15) next in line. Will the Lions just roll with those players, or increase their blitz rate, which currently just sits at 30.9% (16th)?

I have no idea.

Player to watch: Derrick Moore. The Lions’ second-round rookie defensive end has four sacks in his last two games, and is bound to have a ton more opportunities moving forward with Hutchinson out. In the past four weeks, Moore has posted a 68.5 PFF grade, ranking 37th out of 117 edge rushers.

Advantage: Lions +1. I still have a healthy amount of skepticism regarding the Lions’ pass defense, but what they have proven without a doubt over the past month is that they can hold bad pass offenses down. That’s what the Bucs are.

Bucs run offense (10th) vs. Lions run defense (20th)

Tampa has been outstanding running the football this year, particularly as of late. They’ve rushed for over 100 yards in six straight contests and finished with at least 4.5 yards per carry in five of those six games. For the year, they rank:

First in yards per carry (5.0)

Eighth in rush EPA (0.005)

Fourth in success rate (48.1%)

The offensive line can be great at times, but their overall stats are more average than outstanding. They’re 14th in adjusted line yards, 16th in run-block win rate, and 15th in PFF run-blocking grade.

The stars of the show, without a doubt, are the running backs. Both Kenny Gainwell and Bucky Irving are outstanding at creating yardage on their own.

Gainwell:

+1.2 rushing yards over expected per rush (third in NFL)

4.7 yards after contact per rush (first)

Irving:

+0.7 RYOE/r (ninth)

3.6 YAC/r (12th)

According to Pro-Football-Reference, Irving’s 16 broken tackles leads the league.

Despite the very low DVOA ranking, the Lions’ run defense has passed both the eye and statistical test over the past five games. For the year, Detroit ranks:

15th in yards per carry allowed (4.0)

Eighth in rush EPA (-0.102)

Sixth in success rate (36.9%)

So what is dragging them down so much in DVOA? A few things. They haven’t faced particularly good rushing attacks all season. By rushing yards per game, the Lions have faced just a single team (Bills) ranked 15th or higher this year. And while they own a great success rate, they’ve been terrible in short-yardage situations, allowing conversions on 86% of power runs (32nd). Those high-leverage plays are almost solely responsible for Detroit’s low DVOA ranking. Because Detroit looks great in adjusted line yards (third), stuffed rate (sixth), and run-defense PFF grade (fourth).

Personally, I think they’re a lot better than DVOA suggests, but will admit that the Bucs will present the second-biggest challenge of the season.

Player to watch: Irving. He’s extremely capable of carrying defenders, but it’s worth noting that the Lions are outstanding at tackling. They have PFF’s best tackling grade in the league (81.6) and the fewest missed tackles, per PFR.

Advantage: Bucs +0.5. I think this could go in either direction, but because the Lions haven’t been tested like this in months—and they’ll be without Campbell and Hutchinson—I’ll give the slight edge to the Buccaneers.

Last week’s prediction

I’m tempted to throw out last week’s prediction entirely because so much of my preview was about the huge advantage the Patriots’ passing offense had. When Drake Maye was lost on the opening possession, that edge was completely erased. Now, the Lions still did a good job in coverage, but it’s hard to believe that game would’ve looked anything like that if Maye had stayed in the game.

Still, it counts. I got the winner right, but missed on the Vegas line. On Paper is 7-2 overall and 4-5 against the spread.

In the comment section, we had one prediction that was outstanding on just about every level:

Congrats, ascofield68! Here’s your prize.

Do you have trouble sleeping? Do you spend time in the middle of the night worrying about all the “what ifs” in your life? Well, enjoy this new white noise option on your phone:

This week’s prediction

The Lions come out with a +1 advantage, but I think it’s worth pointing out how no team as more than a +1 advantage in any of the four matchups. Just about every single aspect of this game is a coin flip, and my confidence level is very low in any predictions this week. Add in the fact that Mayfield is likely playing through injury, the Lions will be missing Hutchinson but getting back Joseph, and there are just so many factors in this game that make it so difficult to predict.

Still, I’m expecting a low-scoring, tight battle. Lions 20, Buccaneers 16.

lions.headline: Aidan Hutchinson shares thoughts on injury: ‘I always come back stronger’
lions.body:
MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - NOVEMBER 08: Aidan Hutchinson #97 of the Detroit Lions looks on during the second half of an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins at Hard Rock Stadium on November 8, 2026 in (Photo by Logan Bowles/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Detroit Lions All-Pro defensive end Aidan Hutchinson took to social media to deliver a message to fans for the first time since tearing his ACL in Week 10 against the New England Patriots in Germany. Hutchinson’s injury occurred moments after a drive-ending sack of QB Drake Maye, as the star edge rusher leaped in celebration and his knee buckled on landing. The perennial Defensive Player of the Year candidate will require surgery, and his 2026 season is unfortunately over.

Here’s the message Hutchinson wanted people to see:

I honestly can’t believe it. I’ve jumped hundreds of times on a football field and never in a million years did I think this would happen to me.

But even something like this won’t hold me back.

I can ask why over and over again, but it’ll never make sense. All I can do is surrender to the path. Only God knows why and I trust in Him.

Very grateful for all of your prayers and well wishes.

Two things I know for sure:
1. I always come back stronger.
2. That’s the last time I go airborne 😁👍

Hold down the fort til I’m back, boys.

Hutchinson is no stranger to recovering from season-ending injuries. In 2024, he broke his leg and spent several “miserable” days in a Dallas hospital, and gained a new perspective on life. Early signs for Hutchinson are that he didn’t suffer any other significant knee damage, but they can’t be certain until the surgery takes place. If it goes well, he’s expected to have a chance to recover and return to play sometime in 2027, hopefully “stronger,” as he did after his 2024 injury.

lions.headline: NFL Week 11 picks, predictions: Colts vs. Texans on TNF
lions.body:
Indianapolis Colts quarterback Daniel Jones (17) and Houston Texans quarterback C.J. Stroud (7) meet centerfield Sunday, Sept. 27, 2026, after the Indianapolis Colts defeated the Houston Texans 19-17 at Lucas Oil Stadium in Indianapolis. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co

Believe it or not, we’re already in Week 11 of the NFL. Better appreciate the season while it’s still here.

Thursday night could be a tough night to be thankful for the NFL. Not only is it a matchup that doesn’t impact the Detroit Lions in any meaningful way, but it’s also a game that shouldn’t be all that close or interesting.

The 3-6 Houston Texans are hosting the 3-7 Indianapolis Colts.

It’s been a massively disappointing season for both teams. Both went into the season with Super Bowl aspirations. Now, they have a combined 5 percent chance to make the playoffs, according to RBSDM. lions.headline: Lions, Bucs  injury report: QB Baker Mayfield returns to practice, feels ‘ready’ to play
lions.body:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 20: Baker Mayfield #6 of the Tampa Bay Buccaneers looks to pass in the third quarter of the game against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field on October 20, 2025 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images

The Detroit Lions (7-2) and the Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-6) were back on the practice field Thursday, and with the Lions holding a walkthrough Wednesday, this was our first real look at where Detroit’s players stand with injuries.

Note: Any changes from the most recent injury report will be bolded.

No practice

C Cade Mays (low ankle sprain)

Earlier in the week, coach Dan Campbell said he didn’t think Mays would reach a point where he could play this week. With an estimated “no practice” on Wednesday and an official “no practice” on Thursday, it’s probably too late for a player who’s been injured for multiple weeks to return to practice and play in a game with only a few days remaining. Mays is almost certainly out for this Sunday.

Limited practice

RB Sione Vaki (ankle)

DL Tyler Lacy (shoulder)

LB Joe Bachie (knee)

CB D.J. Reed (hip) — won’t rush back, unlikely to play vs. Bucs

CB Khalil Dorsey (ankle)

CB Ennis Rakestraw (shoulder)

Vaki has been nursing his ankle injury for nearly two weeks, but he hasn’t missed any game time and practiced this week, suggesting he could play again on Sunday.

Lacy’s best asset is his ability to stop the run, and with the Bucs grinding out yards on the ground, he’d give the Lions a big boost if he is available to play on Sunday—which sounds realistic based on how coaches have been discussing him this week.

Bachie has been solid special teams depth since being called up to the active roster, but little is known about his injury. If he can’t play, the Lions have five other linebackers on the active roster and Owen Pappoe (elevated for special teams last week) on the practice squad.

Reed is getting some work on the practice field this week, but he is taking his recovery process slowly after rushing back too soon last year. It wouldn’t be surprising to see Reed sit out another week and potentially work toward trying to be ready for the Bears on Thanksgiving.

“I definitely want to make sure I come back and I feel like myself. I don’t want to rush it, especially because our defense is playing well,” Reed said. “So I don’t want to be a hindrance. So I just gotta be honest with myself, be honest with the trainers and my coaches to see if I’m ready to go, whenever that is.”

Dorsey was injured during the Patriots game and needed trainers’ assistance, but he exited the field on his own and is estimated to have practiced on Wednesday, an encouraging sign for his potential availability against the Bucs.

Rakestraw did not appear to suffer an injury against the Patriots, but he played only a few snaps, so the injury may have been nagging. Like Dorsey, limited practices are encouraging signs for his potential availability.

Full practice

S Kerby Joseph (knee)

Joseph continues to take the necessary steps to return to game action this Sunday, as Campbell noted earlier in the week. As long as he doesn’t suffer any setbacks between now and Sunday, expect him to play against the Bucs.

Bucs’ injury report

No practice

RB Bucky Irving (rest)

WR Chris Godwin (rest)

S Antoine Winfield Jr. (ankle)

Limited

QB Baker Mayfield (foot/right thumb) — UPGRADED from no practice Wednesday

DT A’Shawn Robinson (rest)

OLB Yaya Diaby (knee)

Full

CB Josh Hayes (knee)

TE Cade Otton (thumb)

OT Tristan Wirfs (toe)

Bucs QB Baker Mayfield returned to practice on Thursday and has a real chance to play against the Lions on Sunday. Some questioned whether Mayfield would need another week to recover from his foot injury, and after missing Wednesday’s practice, things looked grim. lions.headline: 6 takeaways from Detroit Lions coordinators prior to Bucs game
lions.body:
Aug 2, 2026; Allen Park, MI, USA; Detroit Lions defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard addressed the media at Meijer Performance Center. Mandatory Credit: Paul Barnick-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Detroit Lions coordinators met with the media on Thursday in preparation for their big game against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers this week. Here are six takeaways I had from Drew Petzing, Kelvin Sheppard, and Dave Fipp.

Offensive coordinator Drew Petzing

Kyle Juszczyk inspired how the Lions use Sam LaPorta

Recently, the Lions have utilized a lot of return motions with Sam LaPorta—where he’ll be in motion in one direction during the snap, and suddenly change directions after the snap. Here’s a good example from last week:

The Lions are getting really good at using this "Banana" motion. Fun G/H counter variation with it and it works so well for RB Sione Vaki to follow a lead blocker and get downhill. #OnePride pic.twitter.com/Ho0OGk5En0
— Russell Brown (@RussNFLDraft) November 16, 2026

Petzing revealed that he was inspired by how the 49ers use fullback Kyle Juszczyk—someone Petzing worked with at Harvard—when putting LaPorta in that role.

“You have got to have somebody who’s athletic, who can play on the move, who can live in the gray a little bit because it’s not like when he’s going in full motion, he knows exactly what the look is or exactly where everybody’s lined up,” Petzing said. “And I think Sam does such a good job of navigating that. And then there’s pass game stuff that comes off of it, obviously, which Sam is elite at. So, I think that’s kind of where it came from and why we feel like it really fits us and him as a player.”

Here’s Juszcyzk doing something similar (albeit with no pre-snap motion)—against the Lions—but building some of the pass game stuff Petzing was referring to.

Kyle Juszczyk is so good at this

I-Formation Wide Zone Lead, but the Fullback redirects to the Slide Route 😳 pic.twitter.com/9bv8kAgQze
— Coach Dan Casey (@CoachDanCasey) December 31, 2024

Pass protection imbalance

Our own Al Karsten was one of the first to notice some incredible splits between the first and second half pass protection. In short, the Lions have been one of the worst pass protecting units in the first half and one of the best in the second:

Detroit Lions Pass Protection Entering Week 9:

1st Half
• Sack Rate: 9.0% (29th)
• Pressure Rate: 41.7% (24th)

2nd Half
• Sack Rate: 2.5% (3rd)
• Pressure Rate: 29.2% (2nd)

The Dolphins defense entered Week 9 ranked 28th in sack rate (4.1%) and is somehow making life hell…
— Al Karsten (@FootballGuy_Al) November 8, 2026

The Lions have allowed 21 sacks this season, and 18 of them have come in the first half. Petzing had several explanations for the phenomenon.

“A lot of it is we’ve really ended the last five or six games running the ball probably 70 to 75 percent of the game, which probably has a little bit of hand in that,” Petzing said. “I think settling in is a part of that. I like to think that we wear on people and bring fatigue in the way that we play and the way that we go through a game. So, some of those things could certainly play into it. And then part of it’s probably just chance, a little bit of both.”

Defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard

Tyleik Williams already one of the best nose tackles in football

If you were just box-score scouting, you may overlook the impact of Lions 2025 first-round pick Tyleik Williams. But the defensive tackle has taken his game to the next level, and Sheppard believes he’s already one of the best nose tackles in the league who is still scratching the surface with his pass-rushing abilities.

“I’m seeing one of the best nose tackles in the NFL right now. And things may not show up on the stat sheet but just turn on the tape and show me where an offensive lineman blocks him one-on-one and has success. Rarely to never,” Sheppard said. “And credit to him because he does have a lot more in his toolbox, a lot more in his arsenal where he could be saying, ‘Oh, I need more pass rush.’ He’s never done that. He’s taken advantage of his ops. He knows where we need him for us to play collectively at a high level and he’s doing it.”

Despite his high level of play, Williams has only played in 301 defensive snaps, just under 50%. For reference, Day 3 rookie defensive tackle Skyler Gill-Howard is barely behind him at 288 snaps. That likely has to do with game situation, and the Lions facing more passing situations than run on defense. But even so, Sheppard expects Williams to see his playing time rise soon.

“Are we going to try to find more plays for him? Absolutely. He’s one of our better players right now.”

Roger McCreary has earned his trust

While D.J. Reed remains sidelined, the Lions have leaned heavily on Roger McCreary. Sheppard told an interesting story on why he’s drawn to a player like McCreary—who has his share of doubters, as the Lions are now his third team in the last two seasons. McCreary asked Sheppard not to pigeonhole him as an outside cornerback or nickel—just give him an opportunity to win anywhere.

Now, after a strong couple of games in Detroit, the roles have reversed. Whereas McCreary was leaning on Sheppard to give him an opportunity, now Sheppard is leaning on McCreary to produce on Sundays.

“He’s worked his tail off schematically, physically to do the things that we want done here the way that we do them. And he’s doing it at a high level,” Sheppard said. “This past month, he’s been one of our best secondary players. He’s been one of our best corners, honestly. And I lean on him now. The same way he leaned on me with that trust factor of, ‘Where should I sign?’ I’m leaning on him now, now that things are hitting the road and that’s a player that I count on come Sunday and he’s earned that trust.”

Derrick Moore playing faster

Early in the year, Lions second-round rookie Derrick Moore was not getting many opportunities. After missing significant time in training camp, Detroit wasn’t prepared to give him more than a situational role. Sheppard noted that Moore never complained, just put his head down and put in the work. His role subsequently increased not too long after.

Now, with Aidan Hutchinson out for the rest of the year, Moore will be leaned on more than ever, and Sheppard believes he’s already rising to the occasion—starting with his two-sack performance last week after Hutchinson went down.

“When his opportunity comes, when you operate in that way, when you operate like that, you’re never going to squander that opportunity when it comes because this is what he’s been doing all along,” Sheppard said. “It’s just at a bigger sample size now. But I’m seeing a player that’s playing faster and faster each week. And that was the biggest message to him. We know what he’s capable of. It’s just doing it at a high rate over and over at a consistent basis.”

Special teams coordinator Dave Fipp

No field issues in Munich

Given Hutchinson’s injury and some noticeable slipping on the turf in Munich, Germany, some have criticized the groundskeeping at Allianz Arena for the Lions vs. Patriots game last Sunday.

Don’t count Dave Fipp among them. He believes the conditions were quite similar to that of Lambeau Field.

“I feel like that field reminds me a little bit of Green Bay, like afternoon, evening game when the sun goes down in Green Bay gets a little bit slick, sort of similar,” Fipp said. “If you wear the right footing, I don’t think it’s an issue at all. We had some guys change cleats early in the game because I think they felt like they were slipping around a little bit. You could see it on a takeoff on field block or rush or a takeoff on a punt rush or return. Some of those guys are in three-point stances digging in. But, other than that, yeah, no factor. I mean, both sides are playing on it. I felt like the conditions were great. Yeah, I had no issue.”

lions.headline: Ahmed Hassanein wants to balance discipline, relentlessness in NFL debut
lions.body:
DETROIT,MICHIGAN-AUGUST 22: Detroit Lions defensive end Ahmed Hassanein (99) lines up ahead of a play during the first half of an NFL preseason football game between the Washington Commanders and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Saturday, August 22, 2026 (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images

The stage is set for fan favorite Ahmed Hassanein to make his NFL debut for the Detroit Lions this Sunday against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

Coach Dan Campbell indicated on Wednesday that Hassanein, the team’s sixth-round pick in 2025, will get his first action after starter Aidan Hutchinson suffered a torn ACL last week against the Patriots.

Hassanein has become revered among the fanbase for his intense and tireless attitude, but he also did his part in showing he could be an asset on the field. After missing most of 2025 with a pectoral injury, he shifted positions to Detroit’s “big end” role this year, and thrived both in training camp and the preseason. That culminated with 2.0 sacks and five quarterback hits in three games—including a sack against Joe Burrow and the Bengals’ first-team offense.

Yet Hassanein has been a healthy scratch all season. Detroit has been happy with the depth along the defensive line, and for good reason. The Lions have been able to generate pressure with their front four, and Hassanein had been thriving in his role of scout team defensive end, preparing Detroit’s offensive line for each and every kind of pass rusher they’ve faced.

“When you get him scout team, he wants to do exactly what the opponent does,” Campbell said. “‘Tell me how this guy plays. What are you looking for? What do you need?’ He asks (Penei) Sewell all the time. And then he says, ‘OK, that’s what it is.’ Then he goes to win. He’s trying to win and he works our guys and he’s making himself better. He makes us better.”

Sunday, that hard work behind the scenes will finally pay off for Hassanein’s first NFL action. And to no one’s surprise, he’s thrilled about it.

“I’m ready. It’s been a long time coming, and I feel good about this,” Hassanein said. “I’m going to go out there, all for God, all for the team, and all for my family.”

Hassanein admits the wait hasn’t been easy. With an intense competitor like him, it’s not easy to spend game days watching. But instead of wallowing, he’s been putting that competitive spirit to use in practice, knowing that this organization still very much believes in him.

“I kept preparing. I got to go against Penei Sewell every day. I get to get better,” Hassanein said. “I get to watch other d-ends, see what they do, get to add to my game, see what I’m weak on, what I need to work on. And, man, eventually, I keep going up every week, and I keep making plays.”

Making an NFL debut would be an extremely emotional moment for anyone. And for someone like Hassanein—who literally broke down in tears after his first preseason sack—you better believe Sunday will be a huge day for him. But he knows he can’t let the emotion get the better of him. He needs to bring the intensity, but not let it allow him to lose focus of what’s most important: playing within his role.

“I have to hold my gap, I have to do my job,” Hassanein said. “I have other people relying on me, and I have to execute it every single time. Not, ‘Oh, I’m gonna do my own thing for one play or two plays or three plays.’ That’s not right. All you have to do is just: What’s the call? What’s your alignment? What’s your assignment? And go accomplish it, and go just destroy the guy in front of you.”

lions.headline: The Detroit Lions’ road to a Super Bowl will be paved with adversity
lions.body:
The Detroit Lions’ Super Bowl aspirations took another painful hit, but coach Dan Campbell isn’t interested in letting adversity change how this team pursues a championship.

Following the injuries to Jack Campbell and Aidan Hutchinson, Campbell was asked about the frustration of not having his full arsenal of players available. His response was about as Dan Campbell as it gets.

“If you’re not careful, you lay in bed at night and you start thinking about all the what ifs, and at some point, you just become a miserable piece of shit. And I’m not going to do it. We’re not doing it. I refuse to look at it that way.”

Losing players like Jack and Aidan stings. Of course it does.

“What has happened with Jack Campbell and with Hutch now will not be in vain. We can’t allow it to. They got us to this point. And so what are we going to do about it, man? Are we just going to let it go to waste, or are we going to do something and pick up the slack?”

It’s a motivating response, but there’s something deeply familiar about this message.

Almost six years ago, Campbell stood before the Detroit media for his introductory press conference and laid out the DNA of what he wanted this football team to become.

“This team is going to take on the identity of this city. And this city’s been down, and it found a way to get up. It’s found a way to overcome adversity.”

Then, the kneecaps. Instantly legendary. But the underlying message was laced with wisdom beyond the sound bites: Detroit is going to fight.

And as this team continues to navigate the ups and downs of the Dan Campbell era, I’ve started to appreciate something about the journey that I don’t think I fully understood when it began.

If the Detroit Lions eventually win a Super Bowl, I don’t think it will come through a perfect season or a series of fortunate circumstances. It will come through adversity. It will come through setbacks, difficult decisions, unexpected challenges, and moments of doubt.

And deep down, I believe that’s the version of this story worth having. That’s the version tailor-made for this city.

The light at the end of the tunnel

For most of my life, believing in the Lions required a certain degree of delusion. I gaslit myself into believing some embarrassingly bad football decisions were winning decisions (I was all-in on the 2019 signing of free agent tight end Jesse James).

Then coach Campbell arrived in Allen Park.

The first year and a half was rough. I could spare you from revisiting the details. But I won’t. I want you to remember what it felt like. 3-13-1 in 2021, including Justin Tucker’s record-breaking 66-yard field goal as time expired at Ford Field, an excruciating 16-16 tie against the Pittsburgh Steelers, followed by a 1-6 start in 2022. The Lions had spent nearly two full seasons getting knocked down, but they kept getting back up.

By the end of 2022, the Lions were 9-8 and had won eight of their final 10 games, including the greatest game the Lions have ever played at Lambeau Field, which sent Aaron Rodgers packing.

Dan Miller’s impassioned speech spoke to the whole city, signifying a great shift in mindset.

“Let’s get comfortable with being uncomfortable because you know what uncomfortable is? It means you’re good. It means you have expectations upon you–and now this team does.”

Then came 2023.

For the first time in generations, Lions fans had a legitimate reason to believe they were watching something special. Detroit exorcised demons by winning its first division title since 1993, beat Matthew Stafford and the Los Angeles Rams in the playoffs, and won a second playoff game at Ford Field, beating the Buccaneers to reach the NFC Championship Game.

It was extraordinarily satisfying to watch Jared Goff beat Sean McVay and Stafford. There was something prideful about watching Ford Field become one of the most intimidating home-field environments in the NFL.

The city was unhinged. OnePride was a factor. The team was on the verge of kicking the damn Super Bowl door down.

And, for a moment, it was all right there for the taking.

Detroit led the San Francisco 49ers 24-7 at halftime of the NFC Championship Game. Just 30 minutes away from the biggest game in franchise history.

There it was. The light at the end of the tunnel. Except it wasn’t a light. It was a freight train. The Lions climbed all the way to the doorstep of the Super Bowl, only to get knocked down again.

In hindsight, maybe my mistake was ever thinking that reaching that level of success—that light at the end of the tunnel—meant the hard part was finally over. After the game, Campbell spoke to a reality that, looking back on, I didn’t fully believe or couldn’t truly appreciate.

“I told those guys, this may have been our only shot. Do I think that? No. Do I believe that? No. However, I know how hard it is to get here. I’m well aware. It’s going to be twice as hard to get back to this point next year than it was last year. That’s the reality.”

When the Super Bowl becomes the expectation

After unfamiliar success, I was convinced the 2024 season would be the year.

Sure enough, the Lions got back up off the mat after the loss in San Francisco, went 15-2, and secured the NFC’s No. 1 seed. The offense was dominant, and the team had established itself as one of the NFL’s best.

The gut punches, however, wouldn’t stop. The injuries kept coming. Hutchinson, Alim McNeill, Carlton Davis III, Derrick Barnes, and Malcolm Rodriguez all suffered season-ending injuries. Ultimately, the Washington Commanders ended Detroit’s season in the divisional round.

But I also think something else happened during that period.

For a fan base that had spent decades hoping to see a competitive Lions team, the Super Bowl had finally become the expectation. I know it happened to me.

I believed in what Dan Campbell and Brad Holmes had built so much that I started expecting the Lions to win every single week. That was not necessarily a bad thing. This team had earned that confidence.

Back to Dan Miller’s proclamation to get comfortable being uncomfortable: the uncomfortable feeling can’t fade away as the seasons go by. When Campbell spoke to the reality about the difficulty of repeating success in this league, I should have fully believed him.

See, when you stop feeling that uncomfortable feeling, when the expectation is not complemented with appreciation for the moment and adversity, the edge becomes lost. The fire built up over years of starving for winning dies down.

That uncomfortable feeling is essential.

Back to the ground level

Then came 2025.

Ben Johnson left to become the head coach of the Chicago Bears. While many have called it a sign of betrayal, I think Ben’s deliberate choice to take the Bears job signified more. It suggests, perhaps subconsciously, his true belief: that he is better. That he would build a team better than Campbell and the Lions ever could without him.

And in just one season, he started to make his case. The Lions struggled to recalibrate, injuries continued to take their toll, and the season ended with a 9-8 record and no playoff appearance. Meanwhile, Chicago won the NFC North.

For a team that had spent the previous two seasons establishing itself as the division’s best, watching Ben Johnson instantly bring success to Chicago was humbling. Campbell’s immediate response at his end-of-season press conference, however, was notable. He said he wanted to get back to what the Lions were doing in 2022.

“I want to get back to some of the things we were doing a couple of years ago. And what I mean by that is just getting back to a little bit of what we did at the ground level, just a little bit of the way we train, the way we go about things.”

See, Dan speaks from his gut. He lets his experience and instincts be his compass. I think that quote is representative. His gut told him the team had lost something it once embodied. He recognized that some of the foundational elements that made them who they are as an organization needed revisiting.

Success changed things. Expectations changed. Mindsets shifted. The challenge became maintaining the habits that got them there while continuing to evolve.

From Dan’s perspective, the team needed that reminder.

And perhaps the fans did, too.

Embrace the fight

Here we are in 2026, and the Lions are continuing to get knocked down again, and again, and again.

The NFC North has become the best in football. Detroit, Minnesota, and Chicago are all 7-2, while Green Bay is 6-4. There is no room for error, and the race is on.

Jack Campbell’s and Aidan Hutchinson’s injuries have been difficult to watch. They are difficult to accept. The initial reaction has been to wonder what this team’s ceiling is without two of its defensive captains.

But Campbell’s viral response brought everything back to where this story began.

“If you’re not careful, you lay in bed in night, and you start thinking about all the what-ifs. And at some point, you just become a miserable piece of shit. And I’m not going to do it. We’re not doing it. I refuse to look at it that way.”

It is incredibly valuable to have a leader who understands that a championship pursuit isn’t linear. Dan understands that circumstances will change, often in ways nobody can anticipate.

I believe in him. I believe in the “Grit” philosophy he’s been preaching since he arrived in Detroit.

That doesn’t mean I agree with every decision, every draft pick, or every fourth-down call. It means I believe that a Dan Campbell team will always get back up. The team will have the hunger to compete. The appreciation of the moment. The willingness to embrace the fight.

Why would we want it any other way?

The Lions have an opportunity to make a statement as they host the Tampa Bay Buccaneers in Week 11 and then the Bears just four days later on Thanksgiving.

The Chicago Bears are coming to Ford Field, and the national conversation has increasingly shifted toward the Bears and Vikings.

Good.

Let them have the attention. Let them have the expectations. For decades, I craved that attention for the Lions. But it’s meaningless. In fact, I think I feel more comfortable on this side. And I think Dan Campbell likes it this way, too.

From the beginning, Dan Campbell told the fan base what kind of team he wanted to build. A team that would get knocked down, get back up, and keep fighting. He never promised that the road would be easy. He never guaranteed wins. He promised a team that would take on the identity of its city.

Almost six years later, that message is as true as ever.

If the Lions eventually win a Super Bowl, it won’t erase the heartbreak in San Francisco, the demoralizing injuries of 2024, 2025, and now 2026. Those experiences will be part of the story. I’m not rooting for the injuries. I’m not rooting for the setbacks. I’m not suggesting the Lions need to suffer to win. I’m saying that adversity is inevitable, and how this team responds is what makes the journey worth following.

Embrace the fight. Appreciate the opportunity. Keep the edge.

And when the Lions finally get there, I have a feeling we’ll appreciate every gut punch and every scar for the triumph each represents.
