michigan.headline: No. 4 UCLA at Michigan Preview: Insanity
michigan.body:
The Michigan Wolverines have experienced every type of loss this season, spanning from heartbreaking (Iowa) to frustrating (Minnesota) to disappointing (Indiana) to embarrassing (State) to depressing (Oregon). With two games to go, who knows what sort of misery is in store?? The latest antagonist will be the sport’s newest darling: the undefeated UCLA Bruins and Bob Chesney.

Even after losing Nico Iamaleava, the Bruins just keep winning, having a great shot at the Big Ten Championship Game (again: RIP) and will surely make their College Football Playoff debut. However, despite a 10-0 record, UCLA sits just fourth in the rankings behind multiple teams with losses, perhaps due to less favorable analytics.

For example, SP+ has this team 12th nationally, which is still very strong — and certainly much higher than Michigan at No. 43, which corresponds to an 11.5-point gap between these teams. That is not how Vegas sees things, though, which bafflingly has UCLA favored by essentially a field goal. Nothing is ever off the table, and this game is being played in Ann Arbor, but a lot has to improve for the Wolverines to actually pull off the upset.

No. 4 UCLA (10-0, 7-0) at Michigan (5-5, 2-5)

Date & Time: Saturday, Nov. 21, 3:30 p.m. ET
Location: Michigan Stadium, Ann Arbor, MI
TV/Streaming: CBS

Michigan has now played every Pac-12 addition twice as conference foes…except for UCLA. These schools do have a healthy amount of history, but have not actually met on the gridiron since September 2000, when the Bruins won in Pasadena. Unfortunate timing to finally get UCLA three years into expansion when the program is somehow having a historic season, but this Michigan team might have trouble against anyone right now, so oh well.

Offense: Fool me 10 times…

Everyone already knows the stats, and anyone who has watched even five minutes of the Michigan offense this season knows just how bleak things are on this side of the ball. Going up against the No. 3 defense per SP+ is not going to make things any better, especially when UCLA gives up just 2.67 YPC, good for fifth nationally, and 5.7 YPA (seventh-best).

The Wolverines will struggle to sustain drives against this stout defense, but quick scores are even more unlikely. Savion Hiter’s touchdown was Michigan’s first play over 50 yards this season, and the Bruins have been one of the best defenses at preventing explosives. Jim Harding is probably going to make this offense more effective, but even those improvements might not materialize into anything this weekend.

Obviously, this team’s biggest problem is at quarterback, and the fact that Tommy Carr — he of two touchdowns, three interceptions, and 114 YPG this season — is the best option says it all. UCLA has shot down better quarterbacks than the overwhelmed freshman, and only one opponent has passed for over 6.3 YPA against the Bruins this season. The passing game is not really a viable choice for Michigan.

This is a no-win scenario. The visitors will stack the box and dare Carr to beat them, which becomes even less possible with JJ Buchanan now out. To make matters even worse, UCLA is the only team averaging 2.0 interceptions per game, which will absolutely come into play if Bryce Underwood gets some more snaps. Michigan will not score points unless the defense sets up very favorable field position (or scores the points itself).

Defense: Vegas believes

How on earth, then, can the spread be so low for this game? This is a top-five team in the CFP rankings, borderline top-10 per analytics, facing a team without a quarterback and with a completely disengaged head coach. Apparently there is still a ton of faith in the Michigan defense, which certainly does not match the vibes after surrendering 21 to Rutgers, watching State keep driving down the field, and giving up 31 just last weekend.

Of course, the Wolverines have a ton of talent across the defense and Jay Hill has been the one home-run hire. Everyone on this side of the ball is motivated to improve over the last few weeks, and this game might be a good chance to do that. The Bruins are only averaging 24.2 PPG over their last six games, corresponding with the exit of Iamaleava, and Michigan’s defensive numbers are still very strong over the course of this season.

Ty Dieffenbach has been solid as the replacement quarterback, leaning on the team’s leading receiver, uhhh, Semaj Morgan. He is less mobile than Iamaleava, but he has the ability to take some shots downfield, often to Aidan Mizell, who has 326 yards in the past two games alone. Hill will need his defensive backs to do their job and lock up these receivers, which has not always been the case recently, as the approach should be shutting down the run game and getting after the quarterback, who does have a banged up shoulder.

When it comes to the run game, Anthony Woods has been quite productive, but it is Wayne Knight who grabs the headlines. Against Power Four competition, Knight is third in the nation with 13 rushing touchdowns this year, averaging 88 yards in these games. Michigan will need to find a way to slow him down without giving up the back-breaking plays in the air, which has proved to be a tough ask recently.

Rock bottom looms

So it seems like the offense is completely overmatched and the defense has a chance to at least play to somewhat of a draw; that still gives the heavy advantage to the clearly better team. I remain baffled at the spread, and if I were not in the Michigan sphere, I would not give this game any second thought, as the numbers, the narrative, and the eye test all skew pretty heavily one way.

But since this is a Michigan-centric site, I guess I will take a stab at finding the path for the upset. Clearly the Wolverines must win the turnover battle, and convert all takeaways into points. The run game has not been an asset this season, but a low-scoring contest like the Indiana game seems to be the right path; this defense is better than it has recently shown, and the UCLA offense is not impossible to contain, so it certainly could turn into a rock fight. And maybe the team gets a little extra motivation on Senior Day — plus from the recent humiliations — which makes enough of a difference in the margins.

If that does not happen, though, and the expected result does occur, then we are about to enter a dark week. 5-6 heading into Columbus, with Ohio State suddenly back on the CFP bubble? Yea, not great. For those who are completely over Kyle Whittingham (which seems to be just about everyone), maybe rock bottom is where this program actually needs to be. Still, another flat performance this Saturday will make it a miserable week with The Game ahead.

michigan.headline: Fee Fi Foe Film: UCLA Defense 2026
michigan.body:
Fee Fi Foe Film: UCLA Defense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 20th, 2026 at 9:46 AM

Previously: UCLA Offense
While the UCLA offense is an okay unit, doing its best with middling parts to score just enough to win, the defense is dominating. This is the side of the ball that Bob Chesney knows best, having played defensive back and served as a DBs coach before working as a defensive coordinator at Johns Hopkins. UCLA's defensive rise has been immediate, all the way up to 3rd in SP+ and they have allowed just one opponent to score 25+ points on them. What's powering their success? And what does a Bob Chesney defense look like? Let's take a look.
The Film: To find a comparison to the Michigan offense, I needed to find a bad offense to use. Thankfully, UCLA has played Minnesota in the past couple of weeks, a unit that has generally struggled to move the ball consistently this season. Minnesota also had a bit of (meager) success against UCLA, so we'll get to see how a subpar offense scored 20 points on this vaunted defense. I'll also take a look at tape from the Wisconsin and Purdue games, to see how opponents achieved (some) success through the air and on the ground against this defense.
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

[Ed: Your guess at who's playing for Michigan is as good as mine. I put them in a 5-1 to show Omosigho will roll down to edge, but he mostly does that in their 3-3-5 personnel. Most typical fronts are 3-4 or 4-3 Under. We'll probably see the 3-3-5 vs 12 or Rhino sets, with Barksdale on the bench for a LB.]
Tons of new faces on this defense this year, unsurprisingly. The defensive line is no exception, where there's a hodgepodge of transfers filling most of the spots on the line. Bodies rotate in and out along this front but by snaps, Sahir West and Scott Taylor are your starters at EDGE. West is the more regular of the two, an All-Sun Belt player at JMU last year who made the move with Chesney and is playing SDE at 279 lbs. Taylor is your undersized OLB/EDGE hybrid at just a hair over 240 lbs., a sophomore who was on UCLA last season. He is splitting time with Aiden Gobaira, a former Notre Dame player who was also All-Sun Belt at JMU. At 261 lbs., Gobaira is beefier and plays more on early downs while Taylor plays in a two-point stance on passing downs.
Those aren't the only names at the position, as a pair of sophomores also in the 240s rotate in on passing downs. Anthony Sacca spent last season at Notre Dame while Cole Cogshell was here last year. Sacca has had a role all season, while Cogshell has started to get more run in the last few weeks and I like the latter as a pass rusher. There isn't a superstar among this group (West is the best of the bunch) but there are enough bodies that Chesney has been able to find a way to put the right four guys on the field and call the right plays to manufacture pressure.
As is often the case with transfer-laden teams, I think the defensive tackle spot is the weakest. The starting duo of Texas Tech transfer Amier Washington and Cal transfer Tyson Ford are treading water, just a hair above the cyan line. Ford is the 321 lb. nose, Washington the 281 lb. tackle who is supposed to rush the passer. They are just guys. I actually like Darold DeNgohe a lot more than either of the starters, a Rutgers transfer who played for Chesney at JMU originally and then reunited with his coach. He's the #3 and the most effective in my view, while AJ Fuimaono is the #4 and the worst of the group IMO.
The impact players that give this defense its elite ranking are in the back seven. In particular, it's Sammy Omosigho that stirs the drink. The Oklahoma linebacker was the SAM for the Sooners last season and then hit the transfer portal because he was blocked from a starter's job at MIKE/WILL (replaced on the depth chart by Cole Sullivan). Omosigho transferred to UCLA and has become a rockstar, a do-it-all Swiss Army Knife who is by far the best player on this defense. Our Dangerman for this piece and one of the top defensive players in college football, Omosigho is now on draft radars.
[AFTER THE JUMP: other players]

Omosigho's compadres at LB start with Jalen Woods, a consistent starter at ILB this season and one of the few multi-year veterans on this UCLA roster. Woods has been quite good, which is why it would be quite a loss if he can't go on Saturday after suffering a knee injury against Illinois (Woods is listed as questionable). There are options to replace Woods, notably JMU transfer Trent Hendrick and returner Donavyn Pellot, who have played a fair number of snaps this season as UCLA plays in 4-3 a not-insignificant amount of the time. They probably aren't as good as Woods (though Hendrick is legit) but they can fill in competently.
The secondary features a good group of corners, led by star Scooter Jackson. He's one of the pieces that Chesney inherited from the previous regime and while Jackson was already a pretty good corner, Chesney has polished him up. The result is the B1G's leading defender in interceptions and a very capable coverage man. The other spot will be either Dante Lovett or Virginia Tech transfer Rodrick Pleasant. Pleasant started in the first chunk of the season but suffered an injury against Oregon, which he only just returned from last week. In the meantime, Lovett filled in and played pretty well. Lovett still got the majority of the snaps last week, with Pleasant filling in around him, so Lovett is listed as the starter on the diagram. Both area capable.
UCLA's nickel is Derrick Barksdale, a 5'8 defender who was another Chesney transfer from JMU. Barksdale has been stellar out of the slot, with a pair of INTs to his name. He is backed up by UConn transfer Osiris Gilbert, who has chipped in a fair bit this season but hasn't been up to the standard of the others. Gilbert hasn't played the last two weeks but is not listed on the injury report, FWIW. I'd expect Barksdale to get nearly all available snaps at nickel.
Finally, safety has been just as strong as the rest of the defense. The strong safety is a name I remembered in Malik Hartford, who was always on the depth chart but never played much at Ohio State. He "down-transferred" to UCLA for a chance to start and has been the weekly strong safety, doing so competently. His co-starter Ta'Shawn James (transfer from Iowa State) is a star that shines a bit brighter, with four interceptions and a sterling PFF grade. James doesn't play every snap, ceding some to Utah transfer Tao Johnson and Cal Poly transfer Mason Rivera, who aren't as strong but aren't weaknesses either. UCLA is at their best with James on the field, though.
Base set: For the most part, UCLA was either in a 4-2-5:

Or a 4-3:

How they chose to line those players up, however, varied greatly based on play. We will delve more into that during the clips. They did use six defensive linemen around the goal line:

That's all for personnel packages.
Man or zone coverage: Some of both in this defense. With the amount that they blitz (see below), man coverage makes plenty of appearances on this defense. But there's also zone, as UCLA switches up coverages and disguises pretty well. It's difficult to ascertain the coverage pre-snap and safety rotation post-snap is a big part of the pass coverage. Michigan's offense should expect both man and zone coverage in the game tomorrow.
Pressure: Calling Bob Chesney "Dr. Blitz" doesn't feel right because he doesn't look like a doctor, nor is he old enough to merit such an esteemed label. But UCLA is the blitziest team that I have scouted this season, checking in at 47% of snaps with more than four defenders rushing. That's close to the most that I have ever charted, as ~50% tends to be roughly the limit (no Brian Flores type DCs in the B1G). He sent a lot of heat at Drake Lindsey and as a whole, it had success. On the flip side, ~6% of snaps saw UCLA rush fewer than four defenders, as Chesney occasionally likes to counter his blitzes with dropping eight after showing a blitz. It's a sim pressure and blitzing paradise in the City of Angels.
Dangerman: Among the easiest Dangerman selections I've had this season, the only option here is LB Sammy Omosigho. He's the star of the show for UCLA, as I laid out in the personnel section. The Oklahoma transfer is second on the team in tackles, tied for first in pressures, second in sacks, first in forced fumbles (4 - tied for most in the nation), and has scored two defensive touchdowns. His 91.6 defensive grade makes Omosigho the #4 graded player in the FBS on defense to PFF (min. 157 snaps) and what's remarkable is his consistency: 92.4 in run defense, 84.2 as a tackler, 90.5 as a pass rusher, 84.1 in coverage. There is no area of defense that Omosigho has struggled with this season.
Let's start by showing off that range of abilities. Omosigho is used both as a 5-2 defensive end when UCLA is in a 4-3 personnel package and as a standard inside linebacker. They like using him to pressure the QB, because his abilities as a blitzer and as a pseudo-defensive end rushing the passer are real. Here he is as a blitzer forcing a throwaway:
LB #10 blitzing vs. the C

How about Omosigho in run defense?:

And in coverage:
LB #10 delivering the PBU

That's just from the one game I charted. How about this straight-up pass rush around the tight end for a strip-sack against Purdue?:

Full season highlights:

I looked at a few composite draft boards earlier and Omosigho is now on the cusp of the top 50. It's an amazing story for a player who was good but not this before 2026 in his collegiate career. He left a power conference defense with one of the best defensive minds coordinating it because he couldn't find regular playing time and now is a superstar on the breakout team in college football with an NFL career ahead of him. Hats off to you, good sir.

Overview
The Bruins enter this weekend's clash with Michigan an unblemished 10-0 and it's mostly because of their defense. Here is where UCLA ranks in the following categories:
Total defense: 262.6 ypg (4th)
Passing defense: 176.9 ypg (17th)
Rushing defense: 85.3 ypg (7th)
Per-play defense: 4.18 YPP (1st)
Scoring defense: 14.1 ppg (6th)
Interceptions: 20 (1st)
Fumbles recovered: 10 (3rd)
Any way you want to look at it, this group has been fabulous. The obvious counterargument or moderating influence to these numbers is the quality of competition, as UCLA has played offenses that rank in the following positions in SP+: 114, 88, 65, 71, 20, 91, 108, 112, 109, 52. The one "good" offense that UCLA has played is Oregon and credit to them, they put Dylan Raiola in the torture chamber. That was an impressive performance. But that's the only test so far.
Luckily for UCLA, there isn't a tough offense lining up across from them tomorrow either! But the point is that they have feasted on weaker offenses so far this season. How do they do it? As you can see in those stats, it's mostly by creating havoc. UCLA has a pedestrian 22 sacks on the season but they have generated a huge number of negative plays, fumbles, interceptions, and TFLs because of how they can confuse and overwhelm the opponents. Some of it is talent, but the Bruins throwing many different blitzes at you and lining up in disguising formations put a ton of stress on the opposition.
Those excellent run defense numbers are propped up by clips like this, where UCLA clusters a bunch of bodies around the line of scrimmage, sends the house, and gets a TFL:

UCLA does this constantly. As I said in the base set section, they do lots of weird stuff, lining their defenders up in a variety of different formations. Clustering up to 8 at the line of scrimmage is something they go to in order to create maximum unpredictability for the opposing offense, which produces another run stop here:

But UCLA can also spread out like no tomorrow. Here's a 3rd & long look they used:

That's three down linemen + a stand-up OLB/EDGE (Scott Taylor), then a line of four bodies at 10 yards (LBs/corners), and three DBs so deep they're not even on screen. Moving back to the blitz vs. sim pressures discussion, here you have UCLA in that sort of 5-2 look with Omosigho down on the line and both ends drop (Omosigho/Anthony Sacca), so this ends up being a three-man rush that you wouldn't have been able to spot pre-snap:

And while that ended up with only three rushing, sometimes they do bring the heat:

Nk Derrick Barksdale and CB Malik Hartford are there on the PBU, which leads us to the next talking point. Even if you are able to recognize and pick up which Bruin defenders are rushing on a given play, getting your receivers open against those DBs is not the easiest. The performance of the UCLA secondary has been impressive to date, with CB Scooter Jackson being one of the standout players:

With five INTs, Jackson is among the most prolific corners in college football at turning over the opposing QB but he's not the only one. FS Ta'Shawn James has four interceptions of his own, including this one off of Raiola in the Oregon game:

CB Dante Lovett had to start against Minnesota instead of Rodrick Pleasant with Pleasant's injury and I was impressed by Lovett, providing tight coverage whenever he was targeted:

That trio of Lovett/Jackson/Barksdale at corner/nickel with James hawking over the top and Hartford moving around the box make this a difficult group. They're well-drilled and aren't going to bust much. Indeed, when I looked over the Purdue tape to see evidence of a team that had success throwing the ball against UCLA (Ryan Browne was 19/30 for 378, 3 TD, 1 INT in that game), I saw a lot of nice throws more than bad coverage:

There was a coverage bust on this long catch-and-run touchdown:

But for the most part, this was more about a strong game from Browne throwing the ball (probably his best of the season) than a poor day by the Bruins in coverage:

There is a potential vulnerability down the seam if you can get a linebacker (like Jalen Woods here) singled up on a faster receiver:

But ultimately Brown succumbed at the end and threw a bad ball, intercepted by Pleasant:

"Have good receivers and a QB that's dealing" is my best solution to beating the pass defense of UCLA, which isn't all that helpful for Michigan's present offense in terms of finding a path to win this game. We should also mention the screen game, because that's a handy tool to fight back against UCLA's aggression with the blitz. Minnesota checked into a screen a few times and was able to get RPS+ gains:

But I have to imagine that if that's all you're doing against them, it will run out of its utility pretty quickly. Purdue had some success with the screen game too, but they were also threatening downfield quite a bit. That part is necessary for it to work out as a piece of the gameplan.
As for the run game, only one B1G team has had much rushing success against UCLA and that's Wisconsin. Minnesota rushed for only 3.1 YPC, a few solid runs where some vulnerabilities in the defensive tackle situation were exposed:

Still, it was pretty limited in volume. I don't think the DT duo of Tyson Ford and Amier Washington is all that intimidating, even if I do like Darold DeNgohe as a rotational tackle. Perhaps Jake Guarnera and Manny Beigel can get a few wins against that duo. What I did see from the Wisconsin game is a lot of QB run. Colton Joseph is very mobile and an integral part of the Badger run game overall and it paid off in that matchup:

That's something Michigan could try and replicate but it's worth noting that Wisconsin still only scored 7 points despite rushing for 5.3 YPC (sacks excluded). Why? Joseph is not a particularly good passing QB and the Badger pass offense did nothing in that one (6/16 for 66 yards). No one has been able to marry an effective rushing game that uses the QB run and a suite of different concepts to take advantage of UCLA's aggressiveness (jet sweeps, speed option, outside zone alongside maybe duo on those DTs?) with a strong passing QB who has talent at the receiver position. Someone will at some point, I think. I just don't think that team is Michigan tomorrow afternoon.

What does this mean for Michigan?
As I zoom out from the UCLA defense, I remain very interested to watch this unit take on a good offense. They've posted uniformly excellent results this season, but the caliber of offenses and QBs the Bruins have seen this season haven't been great. Game #12 against USC will be the really interesting game to me, as Jayden Maiava is the best QB that UCLA will have played and Lincoln Riley's offense is better put together and has more weapons than most of the units that this defense has played. That game will be very instructive for seeing how far UCLA can go in the College Football Playoff.
But tomorrow's game? I struggle to see Michigan having a productive day against this group. Regardless of who starts at QB, UCLA is going to send their array of differing pressures at him. On some plays, that'll be a 5-man blitz. Other plays it'll be a four man rush. And sometimes it'll be a 7 or 8 man all-out blitz. You never know which players clustered around the line of scrimmage will be the runs to rush and who will be the ones to drop. It's tricky and complicated and where Michigan's QB and OL situation is, I don't feel good about that whatsoever. A lot of sacks are a risk here.
And it's not like Michigan's WR situation can threaten UCLA's stellar defensive backs. JJ Buchanan is out and Andrew Marsh is... I don't know? The Bruins have some Dudes down there in coverage and if Marsh isn't allowed to play, then Michigan does not have the weapons to test them, nor the QB, nor the OL play. Feels like a nothingburger day in the pass game. The run game could be more productive with a QB activated in the run game like Colton Joseph, but the gains will likely be limited without the threat of the pass. To me this looks like it'll be another classic UCLA game from this season, their defense overwhelms a lackluster offense and the offense cores enough to notch another win. Maybe Michigan's running game will be magically improved and the screen game will be on point to match what the #3 SP+ defense is putting up against you, but I'm not holding out hope.

michigan.headline: Roundtable: Michigan Football vs UCLA
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - OCTOBER 17: A general view of the University of Michigan flag waving during the second half of a college football game against the Penn State Nittany Lions at Michigan Stadium on October 17, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. The Michigan Wolverines won the game 21-18. (Photo by Aaron J. Thornton/Getty Images) | Getty Images

Michigan returns to Ann Arbor one final time this season, as the Wolverines host UCLA on Senior Day (3:30 p.m., CBS). In this week’s Roundtable, Maize n Brew staff members give some takeaways from last week’s game at Oregon, offer up some bold predictions for tomorrow’s game, and much more!

As always, give us some of your thoughts/reactions from last week’s game.

Von: We can’t just rag on how bad the offense was in this one, as the defense was also putrid and put up its worst performance of the year by a long shot. Michigan was out-gained, 326-140, at halftime, and 467-286 for the entire game. Dylan Raiola had 261 passing yards and three touchdowns in the first half alone. GOO! An all-around horrible performance, which is exactly what I expected going out west to play a legitimate team, especially after Kyle Whittingham ran his mouth about Oregon’s NIL.

Nick: I think things were going a bit better than expected actually with the defense able to keep it close for about the first 2.5-3 quarters of the game, but the dam finally broke and Oregon turned it into the blowout that most were expecting. I’m not upset with Jay Hill’s group at all since they’ve been solid all year and have earned some slack. Regardless, this is all overshadowed by the fact Kyle Whittingham has become much too big a distraction in the second half of the season, and Saturday’s loss was just the latest nail in the coffin on his tenure.

Grace: I actually thought the team looked like it was giving a ton of effort, Oregon was just better. I’ll be happy to root for these players no matter where they end up next season.

Kellen: In a depressing way, it’s actually impressive this offense is somehow getting worse week after week. Jason Beck is probably laughing on a comically large pile of cash like Scrooge McDuck after getting that buyout.

Matt: Understandably, it feels as though the team has checked out. Outside of one Savion Hiter run, the offense performed as expected. However, the usually elite defense just didn’t seem to play with any fire. The secondary was obliterated in a way we haven’t seen this season, while the defensive line struggled to get any pressure on the quarterback. This type of game is exactly what happens when your season is already over by early November.

Scotty: That game went about how I expected. The defense was worse than I thought it would be, but it’s clear everyone isn’t mentally in this season anymore, so I’m not very surprised by that.

Charles: It was yet another embarrassment. Burn the tape and fire Kyle Whittingham.

Where does this season rank among the most disappointing in Michigan football history, in your opinion?

Von: In my lifetime, it’s definitely up there. I don’t think anything tops the embarrassment that was the 2014 season, but this is about as close as we’re probably going to get given we currently have a bunch of coaches that don’t care about/care to learn about the traditions of the program, and (some) players that turned on their coaches over a month ago and are probably patiently waiting for the transfer portal to open so they can get the hell out. I just imagine the players being like the old lady in Happy Gilmore — GET. ME. OUTTA. HERE!

Nick: It’s a lot to parse through 147 seasons of this program, but I’d say it’s easily the most disappointing of my lifetime. Last season was bad at 9-3, but at least you could sell yourself on the team’s youth and talent with Sherrone Moore being focused on anything but football. Whittingham was supposed to be able to keep things steady or elevate the program given all he’d done in the past, but instead, this season is not only spoiled, but there are real questions about the future, at least until he’s inevitably (hopefully) replaced at the end of the year.

Grace: It’s one of the worst. When you start comparing stuff to Rich Rod’s tenure, you know it’s not good.

Kellen: In terms of seasons I remember, this is right up there with the 3-9 2008 season under Rich Rod, the 5-7 season under Rich Rod in 2009, and the 5-7 2014 season under Brady Hoke. The same feeling of the players having no faith in the coaching staff just like the fanbase persists. I think those Rich Rod years were worse, but this is pretty damn close.

Matt: I’ve been an avid fan since roughly 2003. I don’t think it’s hyperbolic to say this is No. 1 on the list in that timeframe. This isn’t the worst Michigan team since 2003, as some of the Rich Rod and Brady Hoke teams were certainly worse. However, the gap between preseason expectations and on-field success has never been larger than 2026. Before the season, I thought the absolute floor for this team was 7-5. To already have five losses at this stage is downright shocking.

Scotty: For me, it’s No. 1. I really thought this was going to be a good year, and the talent was there for it to be. Wasted opportunity.

Charles: It’s certainly up there with the most disappointing seasons in school history. Since I started watching Michigan football in 2003, it’s the most disappointing I’ve witnessed. The only seasons that compare are 2008, 2009 and 2014. I think all those teams were less talented than Michigan is this season, and losses to Minnesota and Michigan State have been truly inexplicable. In the end, it would be at least the most disappointing since 2008.

The Wolverines are one win away from bowl eligibility…for the third week in a row. Does making a bowl game even matter? Does it mean anything for the young guys to get the extra practices?

Von: No, the extra practices and the “game” itself would not matter one bit. If the Wolverines somehow win one of these next two games and becomes bowl eligible…why should the team even accept a bowl bid if Whittingham expects a ton of roster turnover this offseason? Whittingham has bashed his current players multiple times this year by saying he’s excited to get the 2027 class (as well as a full portal class of his own) into the program. These current players have so much to play for these next two games, but a bowl game would be useless.

Nick: I don’t think at this point it really matters given much of this roster is going to look different next season. It seems like all parties would just like to get this season over with and I don’t think this program has the Herculean effort in it it would take to win either of the next two games.

Grace: No, making a bowl doesn’t actually seem to make a difference. Beating Ohio State would feel nice, but that’s because it’s a rivalry game. I don’t know getting to six or seven wins really moves the needle.

Kellen: The extra practices would certainly help the young guys in theory, but as long as the current staff is in place, I’m not sure how much of a benefit those extra practices will be.

Matt: I don’t believe it matters. I wholeheartedly believe the Michigan program is going to have a mass exodus to the portal in roughly a week and a half. I also don’t have the faith in at least the offensive coaching staff to develop the younger players.

Scotty: Honestly, I just want this season to be over.

Charles: I feel like I’m in the minority because I know bowl games don’t really mean much in this day and age of college football, but I still love bowl games and think they are an overall positive for the program. Reaching a bowl game wouldn’t make me change my mind on if Whittingham should return for another year because that ship has sailed, but I do think it would be a good thing for the program and players that opt to return. It’s obviously been a pathetic season, but upsetting Ohio State or UCLA and playing in a bowl wouldn’t hurt.

Give us a bold prediction for tomorrow’s game.

Von: UCLA scores an offensive, defensive and special teams touchdown all in the same half.

Nick: I think we’ll see Savion Hiter build on his big game against Oregon and go more than 100 yards rushing again. He’s one of the few spark plugs this offense has, so I’d like to see him heavily featured in this game.

Grace: Michigan scores two touchdowns.

Kellen: UCLA shuts out Michigan at home and Kyle Whittingham gets booed as he exits Michigan Stadium.

Matt: Rod Moore gets in interception in his final game at Michigan Stadium.

michigan.headline: Michigan Hockey Preview: Top-ranked Wolverines face MSU in rivalry showdown
michigan.body:
ANN ARBOR, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 13: Michael Hage #19 of University of Michigan skates with the puck during a game between Penn State and Michigan at Yost Ice Arena on November 13, 2026 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. (Photo by Michael Miller/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

For the first time in program history, Michigan Hockey (10-1) has started two seasons in a row by winning 10 of its first 11 games. After sweeping Penn State out of Yost last weekend, the top-ranked Wolverines now turn their sights to ninth-ranked Michigan State (6-3-1) for this weekend’s home-and-home series.

Let’s dive into the Spartans first.

Michigan State

Michigan State limps into Hate Week after a woefully underperforming, two-point weekend against Notre Dame. The Spartans only have one win in their last four games and have struggled to assimilate their new collection of talented players. However, this team is a sleeping giant and cannot be viewed as anything but.

Sophomores Anthony Romani (7G, 5A) and Ryker Lee (3G, 7A) have powered the Spartans to start the season, and lead a group that ranks No. 17 in scoring offense. Senior Tommi Männistö only has four points to start the year, but the talented Finn has five points in six career games against the Wolverines.

On the blue line, Michigan State’s youth has stolen the spotlight and production. Freshmen Chase Reid (1G, 8A) and Brady Peddle (2A) share the team lead with 15 blocks apiece and make any shot difficult. Reid also leads the unit in scoring.

While the production numbers won’t blow anyone away, their defensive prowess and ability to protect the house have helped ease the burden on their freshman goaltender. With elite support, Joshua Ravensbergen has established himself as one of the best goalies in the country. It’s no small task replacing Trey Augustine, but Ravensbergen’s .940 save percentage and 1.86 goals against average have fans moving on faster than a middle school breakup.

This is the most talented roster in the country, with 17 NHL Draft picks and an NCAA-record nine first-rounders, and it’s only a matter of time until Adam Nightingale’s squad puts it together. But is that time now?

Michigan enters the weekend hotter than fish grease on the offensive end of the ice. Question: How does a team boost its power play percentages? Just score eight power play goals in one series, including seven in one game! Michigan’s power play jumped 13 spots after the series against Penn State and now sits fifth nationally at .326.

The Wolverines continue to be led by the two-headed monster of Michael Hage (5G, 21A) and Jayden Perron (13G, 11A). The dynamic duo — who desperately need a nickname to capture this moment of dominance — remain the top points scorers in the country, with Hage leading the country in assists and Perron leading in goals. Moreover, Perron is five points clear of the next leading scorer despite playing three fewer games. This could be a 1-2 Hobey Baker finish for the Wolverines.

Defensively, Michigan had its ups and downs against Penn State, but the Landon DuPont (14A) hype train has officially left the station. The most decorated recruit in program history is on a historic assist pace, only trails Hage nationally in assists and is getting better every week.

Landon DuPont is on pace for 51 assists

That mark would break the record for U18 defensemen… by 14

It would rank second among all U18s behind Craig Simpson’s 54

Just 10 games in, DuPont’s college career isn’t just good. It’s on historic pace.

A clear and obvious superstar. https://t.co/h7WTG8MBGZ
— Foley (@NHLFoley) November 17, 2026

But Michigan’s breakout player of the year is by far sophomore D-man Drew Schock (5G, 9A). Schock matched his freshman campaign production in just seven games and his confidence on both ends of the ice is palpable.

Between the pipes, Jack Ivankovic’s (.916) slump has reached four games. It’s not time to panic, but Kovie’s worst performance through the first seven games of the season would have been his best over the last four. Against Michigan State, the blue line needs to protect its weary netminder until he can see a few easy pucks into his glove.

Key to the game

Puck possession. Michigan is ranked 32 spots higher than Michigan State in faceoff win percentage. If Michigan can dominate time of possession, it decreases the likelihood of putting the Spartans on the power play and increases the chances of Michigan gaining a man advantage. While this is an obvious advantage for any team, Michigan’s power play is the hottest unit in the country, while the penalty kill is ranked No. 52 out of 62. If the Wolverines can dictate puck possession, they should leave the weekend with no less than a series split.

Fee Fi Foe Film: UCLA Offense 2026

Alex.Drain
November 19th, 2026 at 4:45 PM

For the first time in a few seasons, I get to preview a B1G team that I have never done before, the UCLA Bruins. While Oregon, USC, and Washington were important enough to play Michigan immediately upon entering the conference, lowly UCLA wasn't a priority. A couple years have gone by since the Bruins entered the conference but now we will finally get the first meeting between the two teams since 2000. UCLA is riding high under first-year head coach Bob Chesney, sitting at 10-0 with a #4 ranking in the latest CFP rankings. Today we will take a look at what is making UCLA's offense successful in 2026:

The Film: UCLA lost starting QB Nico Iamaleava for the season on October 10 against Oregon, so we have to pick something after that. Nevada is off the table obviously, giving us Wisconsin, MSU, Minnesota, and Illinois as options. The Badgers have the best defense of the group and are thus most comparable to Michigan, but that game was nearly a month ago and I want to pick something recent. Between Minnesota and Illinois, the latter is more recent so I'll just go with that one as the game to chart, while looking at tape of some of the other contests.
Personnel: Click for big or HERE for PDF.

While Bob Chesney brought quite a few players with him from James Madison, he didn't have a quarterback. So, to the portal Chesney went and he picked up one of the bigger fishes he could find in Nico Iamaleava, a former 5* who flamed out at Tennessee. Iamaleava was middling on the season and then was injured just over a month into it, meaning that Chesney had to go to his backup, Ty Dieffenbach. Dieffenbach didn't have the profile of someone you'd be okay playing B1G games entering 2026, a former 3* recruit who sat two seasons at Pitt and then transferred to Cal Poly, where he had 9 TD to 9 INT in the FCS. Yet Dieffenbach has provided UCLA with enough at QB to keep their undefeated record alive, even if I have some questions about him.
Entering 2026, it looked like RB would be the headliner for this team and indeed, JMU transfer Wayne Knight has been a star for UCLA. His transformation from Space Jam star to a great football player has been surprising to see, but Knight leads the B1G in rushing yards this season with 845, on 5.8 YPC with a whopping 13 touchdowns. He would be the Dangerman for this piece if he had put together a better performance in the game I charted. But we have plenty of tape of Knight's exploits. He's been backed up by Anthony Woods and Javian Thomas, transfers from Utah and Cal, respectively, and they've been fine. Thomas is at 4.7 YPC while Woods is at 5.9, giving the Bruins plenty of talent in the backfield.
The wide receiver position is filled with another grab-bag of transfers. For much of the year, the starters have been a trio of JMU transfer Landon Ellis, South Carolina transfer Brian Rowe Jr., and Old Friend/New Enemy Semaj Morgan. The former two playing on the outside, with Semaj obviously in the slot. However, the recent eruption of Florida transfer Aidan Mizell (the Dangerman for this piece) has changed the picture by giving the Bruins a dynamic deep threat. The other three are fine but not stars to me, Morgan being the most productive, while Rowe and Ellis have chipped in alongside San Jose State transfer Leland Smith. One note: Rowe was sick last week and missed the game, but I would expect him to play this week.
[AFTER THE JUMP: The clips]

Tight end is the spot most obviously lacking in talent to me on UCLA's offense. Josh Phifer came with Chesney and is TE1 and he was a very poor blocker in the game I charted, which matches what PFF has been seeing. TE2 is KSU transfer Brayden Loftin, who I think is better than Phifer but also not particularly good. Wake Forest transfer Harry Lodge is TE3 and has a cyan circle as well. It would be good if these poor blocking TEs could be exciting receiving threats but they aren't, with a combined 14 catches between them (Noah Fox-Flores didn't make the diagram but has four catches).
We are always skeptical of the offensive lines that new coaches like Chesney can put together in Year 1 at a program that is starting over. To Chesney's credit, he's cobbled together a unit that's alright, despite some injuries and moving pieces during the season. The only player to appear in start game this season is guard Carter Sweazie, another JMU transfer. He began the year at RG but then moved over to LG mid-season when Eugene Brooks was demoted. That meant that Julian Armella was taking over at RG and he has played well in that role. This game of musical chairs has ended in UCLA's strongest guard tandem finding the field in Sweazie/Armella.
There was a small change last weekend, with Sweazie playing C and Brooks back in at LG due to an injury to regular center Riley Robell. Another JMU guy, Robell might be the best OL on this line and luckily for the Bruins, his injury doesn't seem serious. The tackles are a bit shakier and also have injury issues, as starting RT Hall Schmidt is injured and his ailment seems far more serious than Robell's. That probably means that South Alabama transfer Jordan Davis is back in at tackle, having started at LT against Illinois, where he began the season before being demoted due to poor play. Davis was rotating at LT with Jensen Somerville, while Jaylan Jeffers got his first start of the season at RT. They rank in the bottom half of the FBS in plays per game, though I will note that Chesney's JMU teams ranked a fair bit higher in plays per game. At the very least I don't think there's anything worth bolding on the scouting report in this section.
Zone or gap blocking: Mostly zone runs from UCLA against Illinois, dueling with inside and outside zone + Counter as their gap play changeup. A decent diet of wrinkles on top of those runs for a fairly diverse scheme but the big three were the meat of their run game.
Quarterback Dilithium Rating (Scale: 1 [Navarre] to 10 [Denard]): One of the feathers in Ty Dieffenbach's camp when he arrived in the City of Angels was his mobility, which, while not overwhelming, is credible. Last season at Cal Poly, Dieffenbach rushed 60 times for 376 yards and four touchdowns (sacks excluded, per PFF). That's a 6.3 YPC clip and it showcased some amount of comfortability using his legs. When Dieffenbach moved into the starting QB role at UCLA, Bob Chesney's staff was aware that running the QB might be something to use as part of the toolkit to make this offense work.
It took them a few weeks to get it going, as Dieffenbach's rushing output was ho-hum the first three games as a starter but it has begun to come online more in the past two games. Dieffenbach rushed eight times against Minnesota for 33 yards, including this scamper:

Then, against Illinois, Dieffenbach rushed five times for 27 yards, like this scramble for a first down:

Neither of those rushing outputs were prodigious but the 4.1/5.4 YPC clips are respectable and with decent speed on display. Dieffenbach's attempts to throw on the run are more mixed (I'll show you in the HenneChart section) but there's enough here as both a designed runner and a scrambler inside Dieffenbach's big (6'6/223) frame that he grades out as a 5 on our scale.
Dangerman: I came into this piece expecting to nominate RB Wayne Knight as the Dangerman and don't worry, he's still a star. But Knight's performance in the Illinois game that I charted was fairly muted, only 56 yards on 18 carries as the Illini kept UCLA's run game in check. So, I decided to use this section to highlight the emerging breakout star on offense for the Bruins, WR Aidan Mizell. A native of Orlando, Mizell played three seasons at Florida from 2023-25 before transferring to UCLA in the offseason. Mizell had 38 catches over those three seasons in Gainesville and wasn't a top-of-the-scouting-report name when he arrived in LA.
Nor was he much of a name on any UCLA scouting report as of a few weeks ago. Mizell had only seven catches on the season at the end of October (though two were bombs... more on that in a moment) and was not a starter on this offense. However, Mizell got an opportunity against the Gophers and made the most of it. He caught just two balls on the day, but both of them were deep shot touchdowns. Here's the first one:

Mizell's stat-line for that game read "2 catches, 150 receiving yards, 2 TD". Yowzers. Chesney couldn't take Mizell out of the starting lineup after a performance like that and the wideout built on that showing with a better all-around effort against Illinois. In that game Mizell had six catches for 176 receiving yards and a touchdown. There was another bomb in that game, on the first drive:

But we also got to see Mizell run more pedestrian routes and show off YAC ability, like on this play:

Mizell has one rush to his name this season, which came on an end-around RB pitch in the Wisconsin game, where he showed off that same ability, weaving his way for 33 yards:

Get this dude the ball and good stuff happens. With the Michigan defense coming off a week in which they were gashed over the top on multiple deep balls by Oregon, Mizell is the last receiver in the B1G besides #4 in Columbus I'd want to play because the deep shot is Mizell's specialty. The last two clips show he has ability to be a playmaker on non-vertical balls, but Mizell has five catches of 50+ yards on the season, out of a total of 15 catches. He has the second-highest ADOT of any B1G receiver with at least 23 targets this season behind only Rutgers' Ben Black. Mizell is going to challenge the Wolverines' secondary on Saturday.
HenneChart: When Ty Dieffenbach committed to UCLA out of the transfer portal, few people had anything to say about his commitment. He was an unknown name to many, a player with no career FBS snaps and a lone middling season at the FCS level. Besides, UCLA had scooped up a big name QB in Nico Iamaleava, which figured to be one of college football's most intriguing reclamation projects. Why would we need to learn about the no-name projected backup?
Because sometimes, injuries strike. That's what happened in the mid-October game against Oregon, when Iamaleava tore his ACL and Dieffenbach was elevated to the starting role. Some wondered if this would end UCLA's season and hopes for a B1G title and a CFP bid, but nope! In fact, Diefenbach's stats are better than Iamaleava's on the whole:
Dieffenbach: 58.8% completion, 9.0 Y/A, 8 TD, 3 INT
Iamaleava: 62.1% completion, 8.5 Y/A, 4 TD, 4 INT
Pretty similar on the whole, slight edge to Dieffenbach.
So Dieffenbach has been able to approximate what UCLA was getting from Iamaleava but what does that actually mean in terms of his abilities as a football player? Right now I'd describe Dieffenbach as an okay college QB fairly similar to Alessio Milivojevic and Drake Lindsey, just in a better situation in terms of the offensive structure around him. Like those guys, he's capable of dropping a dime but also has moments of spotty accuracy and poor decision-making. Given the (nonexistent) expectations for Dieffenbach entering the year, that's alright. Here's the charting from Illinois:

Overview
UCLA's offense enters this week's matchup ranked #27 in SP+, an outfit that is averaging 32.4 points per game and 424.8 yards per game this season. This season has had some wild swings in both directions for the UCLA offense, from hanging 50+ in consecutive weeks on Purdue and Maryland to posting 17 in consecutive weeks against Wisconsin and Oregon. They've won in different ways, grinding out low scoring games and boat-racing teams in shootouts. It's a versatile team and I think given the personnel, 2026 has been a satisfactory output from the UCLA offense.
We can begin to delve more into personnel, because I've talked about Dieffenbach and his new favorite target, but what else does UCLA have to offer? Mizell's emergence is interesting in large part because the Bruins have been looking for a true star at WR and they didn't have it before his last two games. The closest thing to it is a familiar face in Semaj Morgan, who has had a productive season out of the slot, with 41 catches (by far the team lead) for 525 yards and 3 TD. A lot of those plays are just looking to get the ball in Morgan's hands and then letting him go to work, like this mesh concept on 3rd & 7:

This was more or less how we always wanted Semaj to get used, and his YAC potential remains high:

It's not all easy peasy, as Semaj skied up for the game-winner against Illinois on a slot fade!:

For those wondering, PFF has Morgan down for three drops o the season, though they have happened in the last three games. After Semaj and Mizell, my concern mostly evaporates about the remaining receivers. Brian Rowe Jr. is next up with 20 catches for 352 yards ad there's a precipitous drop-off after that. Rowe missed the Illinois game that I charted but I did find this nice diving catch against Wisconsin:

He seems like a perfectly averaging starting WR, with Morgan a bit better and Mizell starting to look very dangerous. The others, Landon Ellis, Leland Smith, etc. are just guys. It's not as good of a WR room as Indiana's but it's way better than MSU's. "Good enough" is probably the best way to describe it.
What is arguably the most crucial piece of the offense is the offensive line, since it both determines how successful the passing game will be and whether opposing defenses can contain the rushing game. The personnel section of this piece lays out all the injuries and the shuffling that this has caused on the offensive line but as we go into this game, I'd expect it to be Jordan Davis, Carter Sweazie, Riley Robell, Julian Armella, and Jaylan Jeffers left to right. The big question is if Robell can go against Michigan, but since he was a game-time decision last week (ultimately held out), I'd assume he is back for this game.
That group is weak at tackle and stronger on the interior. Robell and Armella have been pretty good this season and Sweazie has been competent. The best rushing plays against Illinois were coming from the interior (even with Robell missing that game):

And another:

The tackle situation is sketchier, with usual starter Hall Schmidt possibly suffering a long-term injury. That forces someone you're not as comfortable with in the lineup, as I haven't been big on either Davis nor Jensen Somerville, who has mixed in at tackle during the course of the season. Jaylan Jeffers is perfectly average and the clips against the better defenses look more like "just getting by" than strong play from the tackles. Somerville was beaten here, leading to a strip sack:

It's those pass protection wobbles that can put Dieffenbach in a bad situation he is unable to recover from. And it is also mostly on the OL when the rushing attack has a poor game, like they did against Illinois. The Bruins have been stopped on 4th & short on the ground a couple of times in recent games:

And in the Minnesota game:

UCLA rushed for 4.5 YPC against Minnesota (sacks excluded), a team with a bad run D that has really only been able to stop Michigan this season. They mustered only 3.5 YPC against Illinois, 3.8 YPC against Wisconsin, and 3.6 YPC against Oregon. Better showings on the ground are extant but against that group of better opponents, it has been tough sledding, as in the clips show above. Which is a bit of a bummer because RB Wayne Knight rocks when you give him a chance:

Watch out for the KnightCat:

Knight reminds me a bit of Jonah Coleman from Washington, one of my all time favorite backs (now having a nice rookie season in Denver) and a legendary Short King. The other RBs, headlined by Anthony Woods, are fine too but Knight is the man. If you can't win the battle up front, the RB talent is going to rip you apart. But if you can, and better defenses have been able to, there isn't enough talent at QB and in the receiving room to get around those problems.
The tight ends are also decisively mid, which is one final note. The blocking from Josh Phifer has left a lot to be desired and there isn't a standout blocker in the positional group. None of them have becoming major recieving threats either (Noah Fox-Flores might be the best receiver of the group?), again limiting the weapons at Dieffenbach's disposal. The skill position talent is a little weak, which is probably to be expected in the first season of a program rebuild.

What does this mean for Michigan?
At least on offense, this UCLA team reminds me a lot of the 2024 Indiana team. In that I would describe them as "fake good", a unit that is getting what they need to win each week, but largely against subpar opponents. 2024 Indiana was similar, improving dramatically in year #1 of Curt Cignetti and putting together a (then) dream season to make the CFP but you could tell from watching them that they were not as good as the record indicated. This isn't a slur on Bob Chesney, because he took over a bad team with limited resources and an empty cupboard. Having them in this position is a testament to his coaching ability and big improvements in year #1 are generally the clearest indicator of a superstar head coach.
But this offense doesn't have the horses to be "real good" and they seem a bit like a paper tiger to me. At least when compared to the old threshold to be a national title winner (who knows anymore... few CFB teams are impressive these days). Their OL is beat up and has been average against their schedule. Their QB is doing better than expected but still isn't great and was a middling FCS QB one year ago. They have a great RB and an increasingly exciting deep threat receiver, plus getting the most possible out of Semaj Morgan, but there isn't a ton of elite talent here. I would expect a good defense to keep the Bruins to a low-scoring afternoon, as Wisconsin and Oregon did.
Is Michigan a good defense anymore? I don't know. If their secondary is as scrambled as it was last week, they will give up big plays and probably fall in an insurmountable hole. But we've seen Michigan play better than that and I'd think Michigan's DL can win the battle in the trenches against UCLA's OL. Keep the running game in check, get some pressure on Dieffenbach, not impossible to produce turnovers that allow you to win this game. All that said, UCLA has a lot more to play for and presumably will be 1) more focused and 2) better coached. I'd expect a moderate output on offense from UCLA.

msu.headline: Spartan Hockey…What’s Wrong?
msu.body:
SOUTH BEND, IN - NOVEMBER 13: Notre Dame Fighting Irish goaltender Patrick Quinlan (32) makes a stop on goal during a men's college hockey game between the Michigan State Spartans and the Notre Dame Fighting Irish on November 13, 2026 at the Compton Family Ice Arena in South Bend IN. (Photo by Joseph Weiser/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images

Spartan hockey has gotten a bit spoiled in the last few years. Very solid teams, deep teams, and veteran leadership all helping MSU to an extremely successful yet slightly disappointing three-year run. This year, MSU is off to a slow start, and having just been swept by ND in their B1G opener, they look to regroup against their rivals and top team in the country. The ultimate question remains, what is wrong? With a team loaded with NHL talent, why does MSU look unlike themselves? We are going to dive in and see if we can figure it out.

We all knew heading into this season that this was going to be a young and inexperienced team. Talent is there, but experience is important. There are still some veterans on the team but not the number that have been in previous seasons and the experiences those veterans had in good times and bad went a long way. This team is very much still working on its chemistry and it takes time, but hopefully, that time comes soon.

One of the main concerns is the offensive struggles. This is something Nightingale has spoken on and is trying to fix. The team started off in exhibition and opening weekend finding the back of the net 4-6 times a night. Since then, the offense is struggling and in turn the record shows it. Puck movement has been lackluster and that may very well be a chemistry thing in knowing when a teammate is going to be somewhere before they are there. The Spartans have also struggled in taking the zone and stretch passes from the defense are basically nonexistent. Former MSU defenders like Matt Basgall were fantastic at the stretch pass and giving forwards quick opportunities in open ice. It is a skill set still under development with the current roster. MSU is getting stuck between the blue lines and unable to create real scoring chances at the level of years past. Nightingale said recently they need to create more offense by getting to the difficult areas of the ice. They need to get quicker and be scrappier in those areas to control the puck to open up possibilities for passes and one timers.

Goaltending has actually been quite good. The highly touted freshman Joshua Ravensbergen has been solid. His weakness has been shutting down the power play. That leads into another area that can be cleaned up and that is playing more disciplined. Staying out of the box, especially in crucial times in games is an element that can and should be cleaned up soon. This weekend against the weasels will be a good test. They will be bated into scrums, and they will need to stay out of the box to avoid the opponent’s hot power play and potent offense.

Every young team experiences growing pains. It is one reason why the NHL Draft model is something other sports should look at. The benefit of drafting a player and having them work out their kinks at the college level is very good developmentally for the players. With all the NHL talent on MSU, we are seeing first hand the need to develop their games. Ryker Lee has yet to get hot. He’s second on the team in points but he’s struggled to find the back of the net this season. With back to back years of Howard and Stramel’s goal scoring, we are feeling the drop in that star shooter. Romani has been the closest to taking that role and will hopefully catch fire soon.

MSU has been in the top 3 the last few years and had 1-seeds in the tourney only to get bumped early. Maybe some regular season bumps and the work to find the chemistry will strike at the right time. You just have to make the tourney; once there, it is anybody’s game. I wouldn’t count this team out yet, not with its talent and coaching staff. A sweep this weekend would be amazing but even a split would give this team some swagger back and perhaps get them trending in the right direction. Early season punches like the ND series can be useful if you grow from them. The showing this weekend will give us all a good idea of what the rest of the season will be like.

msu.headline: Getting To Know The Enemy: 6Qs About The Oregon Ducks
msu.body:
EUGENE, OR - NOVEMBER 14: Dylan Raiola #8 of the Oregon Ducks stands in the backfield during the 1st half of a game between the Michigan Wolverines and Oregon Ducks at Autzen Stadium on November 14, 2026 in Eugene, Oregon. (Photo by Al Sermeno/ISI Photos/ISI Photos via Getty Images) | ISI Photos via Getty Images

Happy Thursday, TOC Nation. Our Michigan State Spartans Football Team are officially out of bowl contention.  But tomorrow night is Senior Night and we still want to show our support for the team before the lights at Spartan Stadium are shut off for the year.  I sat down with Thomas Cicansky from Addicted To Quack for a little Q&A.  Let’s see what he had to say.

The Only Colors: Oregon was #2 in the preseason poll.  At the time, were you a believer in that ranking?  Did you see the Ducks as a contender for the national championship?  Without foreseeing a major injury (i.e. Dante Moore), what was the floor for this team?

Thomas Cicansky:  Before the season I was 100% a believer in the Ducks and their ranking. The 3 previous
years coming into this season the Ducks:

Recruited at a Top 5 level out of high school and the portal

Finished in the top 6 of the final AP poll

On top of that, a ton of the team that made it to the semifinals in 2025 was returning for 2026 including a QB that turned down being a 1st round draft pick. I was fully bought into this potentially being the year for Oregon and the absolute floor was 9-3. Which as we sit here today is now the best-case scenario so that is a pretty good way to sum up how this season has gone relative to preseason expectations.

TOC: Oregon got by Boise State in the opener and then fell to Oklahoma State in week 2.  What did you learn about your team from those 2 games?

TC: I learned a lot as my expectations were sky high and the team was not even coming close to living up to those expectations. I’ll provide the most critical thing I learned about the team on each side of the ball.
Offense
I learned our O-Line coach, Alique Terry, had essentially been running a Ponzi scheme with his unit since being hired for the 2023 season and this year was the year the funds dried up. If your readers like, I can recount the entire story with this unit since his hiring in the comments if anyone is interested. But the short version is his first 3 seasons he was able to get by with players he inherited and transfers. But 2026 was going to be the
test of him as a developer with highly recruited O-Linemen and the first two weeks it was a complete and utter failure. The O-Line couldn’t move Boise State or Oklahoma State in the run game and was routinely letting pressure get home against 3-man rushes. They were just physically overwhelmed by teams they absolutely shouldn’t have been overwhelmed by.
They improved physically since the UCLA game, but there are still lots of assignment errors and poor technique that very much limit Oregon’s rushing attack.
Defense
This defense, while talented, was making a lot of mental errors and our new coordinator was blitzing too much. Luckily this has been cleaned up a lot from the first two weeks of the season, but the defense is still good for about 1 goofball play per game that allows a super explosive play.

TOC: QB Dante Moore suffered that nasty head injury in game 4 and is out for the year.  Dylan Raiola, who was the starter at Nebraska the last 2 seasons and was the #1 QB in the 2024 cycle, has taken over.  How is he different from Moore?  What are his strengths and weaknesses?

TC: It’s interesting you framed your question this way because the biggest and most relevant difference between Moore and Raiola might be both Raiola’s greatest strength and greatest weakness.
The major difference between the two are their mechanics. Dante Moore might have the cleanest mechanics and throwing motion I have literally ever seen and it’s why he still might be a first-round pick despite hardly playing this year.
Meanwhile, Dylan Raiola, when faced with an ounce of pressure, doesn’t step into his throws and fully relies upon his upper body. The internet thinks it’s because Patrick Mahomes is his idol, but the real reason is Raiola played catcher in baseball growing up and so from his amateur sporting career, he was used to making throws from his knees or throws that are entirely dependent on the upper body.
This is probably his greatest strength because when the pocket has completely collapsed, he can still get off a bomb downfield without having to step into his throw. The game winning touchdown against USC and the first touchdown against Michigan are great examples of this.

However, this also can get Raiola into trouble sometimes because he isn’t planting and throwing with a strong lower half so these balls tend to float into the secondary. When a receiver isn’t wide open the ball hangs up in dangerous space. His 2nd pick against UCLA is a memorable example of this.

TOC: Give us one name on offense and one on defense that MSU fans are certain to hear a lot of on Friday night.  What makes those guys so good?

TC: Offense
Dierre Hill Jr. is the lightning to Jordon Davison’s thunder in Oregon’s backfield. Davison has been hurt the last two and half weeks meaning Dierre has needed to be both Thunder and Lightning and he is more than capable of being a bell cow running back when called upon. Davison might be back this week, but if he isn’t, Dierre will get a lot of work and when Dierre Hits 6th gear, it’s special.
Defense
Matayo Uiagalelei is an incredibly well-rounded defensive end/OLB. He doesn’t have elite quick twitch pass rushing ability, but he can bull rush or use speed when rushing the passer and has been setting a great edge in the run game this year. Oregon’s other 4th year defensive end/OLB Teitum Tuitoti suffered a season ending injury at the end of the Ohio State game so the end opposite Matayo was filled by committee last week against Michigan. Uiagalelei hardly left the field and I expect will hardly leave the field Friday.

TOC: Oregon is favored by 15.5 points over on FanDuel.  What would it take for Michigan State to come out on top?

TC: If your readers are confused why Oregon lost to Oklahoma State and Illinois but have beat USC and Ohio State by 2 TDs, it’s actually a very simple explanation and it’s how Michigan State has a legitimate shot in this game despite the point spread. It all comes back to that offensive line I was lamenting earlier. That unit is incredibly inconsistent meaning Oregon has this all or nothing inconsistent offence.  Any given game they are capable of scoring 40+ or being held to less than 17. If defenses make mistakes or can’t cover for 2 seconds Oregon can light it up with explosive passing plays. But if defenses are disciplined and have a plan for keeping
everything in front of them, Oregon can’t counter and efficiently march down the field.
I think that’s Michigan State’s path to victory. Keep everything in front of them, force Oregon to have to try to march the field, and on third and long maybe Anelu Lafaele can create some pressure that forces Raiola into turning the ball over to spark the Spartan offense.

TOC: Predict the final score.

TC: From afar, I’ve been impressed with Michigan State’s defense this year and I think Joe Rossi will understand the assignment for the best way to slow down Oregon. On a short week travelling 3 time zones, I think the max amount Oregon will score is 31 but probably closer to 27-24ish.
But the problem I foresee for the Spartans is the other side of the ball. This Oregon defense has really improved over the course of the season and has done so against strong offenses. Provided Oregon takes care of the ball and makes Michigan State have to go 65+ yards each drive, I feel pretty confident Oregon can hold Michigan State to 13 or less.
I think I’ll settle on 24-10 Oregon.
I’ve learned to expect the unexpected with the 2026 Oregon Ducks so definitely not taking the win for granted.

TOC: Aside from former athletes (that includes Phil Knight since he was on the track & field team), who is Oregon’s most famous alum?

TC: This is tough because Oregon is an athletic school. We take a ton of pride in our Track, Diamond sports, and basketball. But excluding athletes, the first that came to my mind is actor Ty Burell, who played the best character on Modern Family, Phil Dunphy. But other famous actors as well include Kaitlin Olson and Sam Elliot.
